story: When Bhima caught the bull into which Shiva had transformed, it sank into the ground and reappeared in five parts, the face emerging at Rudranath.

name: Madhyamaheshwar Temple
deity: Shiva, worshipped here as his navel and belly
significance: A Shiva temple at about 3,497 m in the Garhwal Himalaya of Uttarakhand and one of the five shrines of the Panch Kedar pilgrimage. Its design resembles those at Kedarnath and Tungnath.
story: The navel and stomach of the bull-form of Shiva are said to have surfaced here after the animal broke apart in Bhima's grasp.

name: Kalpeshwar Temple
deity: Shiva, worshipped here as his matted hair (jata)
significance: A Shiva temple at about 2,200 m in the Urgam valley, the fifth of the Panch Kedar shrines and the only one open to pilgrims all year. Its priestly line was appointed by Adi Shankara.
story: The matted locks of the bull-form of Shiva are said to have appeared at Kalpeshwar, where the Pandavas then raised a temple.

name: Jageshwar Temples
deity: Shiva, with shrines to Vishnu, Shakti goddesses and Surya
style: Nagara (North Indian), with Valabhi and latina variants
significance: A Himalayan group of more than 125 stone temples in Almora district, dated between the 7th and 14th centuries and protected by the Archaeological Survey of India. Long a centre of Pashupata Shaivism, the cluster is unusual in that many shrines appear to be memorials rather than working places of worship.

name: Baijnath Temple, Uttarakhand
deity: Shiva as Vaidyanatha, lord of physicians
significance: A 12th-century Katyuri temple complex on the bank of the Gomati in Bageshwar district, now a Monument of National Importance and a stop on the Shiva Heritage Circuit. Besides Shiva it houses images of Parvati, Ganesha, Chandika, Kubera, Surya and Brahma.
story: Shiva and Parvati are said to have been married at the confluence of the Gomati and the Garur Ganga here.

name: Katarmal Sun Temple
style: Katyuri stone construction with carved wooden doors and panels
significance: A rare 9th-century temple to the sun god in Almora district, built by the Katyuri king Katarmalla and surrounded by 44 smaller shrines. It is a Monument of National Importance protected under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act of 1958.

name: Manibandh Shaktipeeth (Gayatri Temple, Pushkar)
significance: One of the 51 Shakta pithas, standing at the foot of Gayatri hill (Puruhuta) beside Pushkar, roughly 11 km north-west of Ajmer. It is venerated as the place where the wrists of Sati came to rest.
story: When Vishnu's discus scattered Sati's body across the subcontinent to end Shiva's grief, her wrists (manibandh) fell on this hill.

name: Chitai Golu Devta Temple
deity: Golu Devta (Goljyu Maharaj), revered as an incarnation of Bhairava
significance: The best-known shrine of Golu Devta, a regional god of justice worshipped throughout Kumaon and Garhwal and treated as a form of Bhairava. It stands on the ridge at Chitai outside Almora and draws petitioners who bring their grievances to the deity.
story: A prince born to King Halrai was cast into the Gori river by jealous co-queens and rescued by a fisherman; he later returned to expose the injustice and was deified as the god of justice.

name: Kainchi Dham
significance: An ashram and temple complex in the Kumaon hills established by the saint Neem Karoli Baba in 1964 on land donated by a local devotee. It draws large numbers of Indian and Western visitors and is widely known through the saint's association with figures in the technology industry.

name: Surkanda Devi Temple
style: Himalayan stone shikhara topped by a trident
significance: A Shakta pitha perched at about 2,756 m above Kaddukhal near Dhanaulti in the Garhwal Himalaya. It is counted among the seats where a part of the goddess Sati is believed to have fallen, and is reached by a steep walk from the road head.
story: After Sati immolated herself and Shiva carried her body in grief, Vishnu dismembered it and her head is said to have fallen on this peak.

name: Adi Badri
dynasty: Late Gupta; foundation traditionally attributed to Adi Shankara
significance: A cluster of small stone shrines at Adibadri in Chamoli district, some 17 km beyond Karnaprayag, counted among the Sapta Badri. Assigned to the late Gupta period, it gave pilgrims a place to worship Vishnu when the high shrine at Badrinath was shut by snow.

name: Har Ki Pauri
dynasty: Vikramaditya (traditional); later British-era and modern expansion
significance: The principal bathing ghat of Haridwar, at the point where the Ganga leaves the mountains for the plains. It is the ritual centre of the city's Kumbh Mela and of the daily evening Ganga aarti, and tradition credits its construction to King Vikramaditya.
story: The pool here, Brahmakund, is said to be where Garuda let fall drops of the nectar of immortality.

name: Mansa Devi Temple
significance: A hilltop shrine on Bilwa Parvat in the Sivalik range above Haridwar, counted among the town's Panch Tirth and regarded as a Siddh Peeth where wishes are granted. It is reached by a cable car or a footpath from the city.
story: Folklore holds that Mansa, born of Shiva's mind, was raised as an ordinary girl and won divine power through austerity.

name: Chandi Devi Temple
dynasty: Suchat Singh of Kashmir; image attributed to Adi Shankara
significance: A Siddh Peetha on Neel Parvat across the Ganga from Haridwar. The present building was raised in 1929 by Suchat Singh of Kashmir, while the principal image is traditionally said to have been installed by Adi Shankara in the 8th century.
story: The goddess Chandi is said to have rested on this hill after killing the demon kings Shumbha and Nishumbha.

name: Vishnuprayag
significance: The confluence of the Alaknanda and the Dhauliganga, and the first of the five Panch Prayag confluences on the Alaknanda. A Vishnu shrine stands beside the meeting of the rivers on the road to Badrinath.
story: The place is named for a belief that the sage Narada meditated here and Vishnu appeared before him.

name: Nandaprayag
deity: Sacred confluence of the Alaknanda and Nandakini
significance: The second of the Panch Prayag, where the Nandakini joins the Alaknanda in Chamoli district. The town was historically the capital of the Yadu kingdom and is a halt on the Badrinath pilgrim road.

name: Karnaprayag
significance: One of the Panch Prayag, at the confluence of the Alaknanda and the Pindar in Chamoli district. A temple of the goddess Uma stands at the meeting of the rivers.
story: Karna of the Mahabharata is believed to have worshipped the sun god at this confluence.

name: Rudraprayag
significance: One of the Panch Prayag, where the Mandakini flowing down from Kedarnath meets the Alaknanda. The Rudranath temple, dedicated to Shiva in his Rudra aspect, stands at the confluence.
story: The sage Narada is said to have meditated at the Narad Shila here to learn music from Shiva.

name: Devprayag
style: Massive stone masonry, pyramidal form with a white cupola
significance: The last of the Panch Prayag, where the Alaknanda and the Bhagirathi join and the river continues as the Ganges. Above the confluence stands the Raghunathji temple, a stone shrine of pyramidal form capped by a white cupola.

name: Sankat Mochan Hanuman Temple
deity: Hanuman (as Sankat Mochan, remover of troubles)
significance: Varanasi's foremost Hanuman temple, traditionally founded by the poet-saint Tulsidas in the early 16th century. It is closely tied to the composition of the Ramcharitmanas and remains one of the busiest shrines in the city.
story: The temple is said to stand on the exact spot where Tulsidas had a vision of Hanuman.

name: Durga Mandir (Durga Kund Temple)
significance: An 18th-century Durga temple beside the Durga Kund tank in Varanasi, built at the expense of the Bengali queen Rani Bhabani of Natore. Its red-and-ochre exterior and adjoining stepped tank make it one of the city's most recognisable shrines.
story: The temple is said to commemorate Durga appearing on her lion to help the Kashi Naresh defeat invading kings, after which she promised to guard Varanasi.

name: Tulsi Manas Mandir
style: White marble, with the Ramcharitmanas engraved on the walls
significance: A white marble temple built in 1964 by the Sureka family at the place where Tulsidas is believed to have composed the Ramcharitmanas. Verses and scenes from that work are carved across its interior walls.

name: Shri Radha Rani Temple (Ladli Ji)
deity: Radha and Krishna, worshipped together as Shri Laadli Lal
dynasty: Bir Singh Deo; earlier structure associated with Narayan Bhatt and Raja Todar Mal
style: Rajput, in red sandstone with carved arches and domes
significance: The hill temple of Radha at Barsana, built in red sandstone in 1675 and the focus of the town's Radhashtami and Lathmar Holi festivals. It is among the principal Braj pilgrimage sites.
story: Radha's father Vrishbhanu is said to have made his home on the Bhanugarh hill at Barsana after leaving Kamsa's Mathura.

name: Prem Mandir
significance: A large modern marble temple complex at Vrindavan, begun in 2001 and inaugurated in 2012 at the initiative of Jagadguru Kripalu Maharaj. Its 22-hectare grounds hold life-size tableaux of Krishna's pastimes and a pillar-free satsang hall.

name: Radha Vallabh Temple
significance: The principal seat of the Radha Vallabh Sampradaya in Vrindavan, built in 1585 by Sundardas Bhatnagar under the guidance of Hith Harivansh Mahaprabhu with support from Akbar's court. It is among the oldest surviving temples of the town.
story: The image is said never to have been carved but to have been given directly by Shiva to a devotee named Atmadev.

name: Krishna Balaram Mandir (ISKCON Vrindavan)
significance: One of the largest ISKCON temples in the world, opened at Raman Reti in Vrindavan in 1975 under A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada. Its central altar holds Krishna and Balarama, and a marble samadhi shrine to the founder stands in the compound.

name: Vishram Ghat
significance: The central bathing ghat on the Yamuna at Mathura, where the town's circumambulation pilgrimage begins and ends. Its steps and shrines were built up over centuries by noble and royal patrons.
story: Krishna is said to have rested here after killing Kamsa, which gives the ghat its name, the ghat of rest.

name: Daan-Ghati Temple
significance: The main temple of Govardhan town, standing at the Daan Ghati pass through Govardhan Hill. It is a principal halt on the Govardhan parikrama and the focus of the town's Govardhan Puja observances.
story: Krishna is said to have raised Govardhan Hill on his little finger here to shelter the cowherds from Indra's storm.

name: Shakumbhari Devi Temple
significance: A Siddhpeeth in the Shivalik foothills of Behat tehsil, Saharanpur district, dedicated to the goddess of vegetation and nourishment. It is one of the larger pilgrimage centres of northern Uttar Pradesh.
story: When the demon Durgamasura brought a hundred-year famine, Adi Shakti appeared as Shakumbhari, whose tears fell as rain and who fed the world with food produced by her own power.

name: Naina Devi Temple
significance: A hilltop Shakta pitha in Bilaspur district overlooking the Govind Sagar reservoir, reached by road and by cable car. It is revered as the place where the right eye of the goddess Sati fell.
story: A Gurjar boy is said to have found the site when his white cow shed her milk over a stone, and the goddess then revealed herself to him in a dream, prompting Raja Bir Chand to build the temple.

name: Bajreshwari Mata Temple (Brajeshwari Devi)
deity: Durga as Vajreshwari, goddess of the thunderbolt
dynasty: Modern reconstruction; earlier shrine ascribed in legend to the Pandavas
significance: A Shakta pitha at Kangra town, counted among the fifty-one seats of the goddess and one of the most visited temples of Himachal Pradesh. The present building replaced the shrine destroyed by the 1905 Kangra earthquake.
story: The left breast of Sati is said to have fallen here when Vishnu divided her body into fifty-one parts.

name: Baijnath Temple
deity: Shiva as Vaidyanath, lord of physicians
dynasty: Built by the merchants Ahuka and Manyuka in the reign of Jaya Chandra; renovated under Sansar Chand
significance: A stone Nagara-style Shiva temple of 1204 CE at Baijnath in Kangra, protected by the Archaeological Survey of India. It came through the 1905 Kangra earthquake with little damage and remains in worship.
story: Ravana is said to have set down a Shiva lingam here while carrying it to Lanka, and out of respect for his devotion the town does not celebrate Dussehra.

name: Bhimakali Temple
builtDisplay: 13th c.; new tower rebuilt in the 1920s
style: Kath-kuni timber-and-stone, blending Hindu and Buddhist forms
significance: Counted among the fifty-one Shakta pithas, this hill shrine at Sarahan was the tutelary temple of the rulers of the former Bushahr state. Its twin towers of interlocked timber and stone make it one of the best-known examples of Himachali kath-kuni building.
story: Devotees hold that the ear of Sati fell here when Shiva carried her dismembered body across the earth.

name: Hidimba Devi Temple
style: Tiered wooden pagoda with a 24 m shikhara over a cave shrine
significance: A wooden temple in the deodar forest of Dhungri, Manali, raised over the cave where the goddess is said to have meditated. It is the focus of the town's spring fair and of Navaratri worship, and is prized for its carved timber doorway and tiered roofs.
story: Hidimbi married the Pandava Bhima after he killed her brother Hidimb, and their son was the giant Ghatotkacha.

name: Manimahesh Lake
style: Small shikhara-style shrine at the lakeside
significance: A glacial lake at about 4,080 m below the Manimahesh Kailash peak, held sacred to Shiva and second only to Lake Manasarovar in regional esteem. Its annual Manimahesh Yatra draws large numbers of Gaddi and other Hindu pilgrims.
story: Shiva is said to have performed centuries of penance here, the lake forming from waters that sprang out of his matted hair.

name: Lakshana Devi Temple
style: Late Gupta wooden temple on a sandhara plan
significance: One of the oldest surviving wooden temples in India, commissioned by Meru Varman at his hill capital of Bharmour and still holding its 7th-century brass image of Durga. Its carved timber doorway and ceiling preserve early Shaiva and Vaishnava imagery rarely found intact elsewhere.

name: Jakhu Temple
significance: An old Hanuman shrine on Jakhu hill, at 2,455 m the highest point in Shimla. A 108-foot statue of Hanuman erected in 2010 has made it one of the city's most visited landmarks.

name: Baba Balak Nath Temple (Deotsidh)
significance: The principal shrine of Baba Balak Nath, a folk deity widely venerated across Himachal Pradesh and Punjab, set in a hilltop cave at Deotsidh in Hamirpur district. Pilgrims come in largest numbers during the month of Chaitra.
story: The deity is said to have been born to a Gaur Brahmin family at Girnar Parbat before settling in the Himachal hills.

name: Renuka Lake Temple
significance: The largest lake in Himachal Pradesh and a Ramsar wetland since 2005, revered as the embodiment of the goddess Renuka, mother of Parashurama. A five-day fair each year around Prabodhini Ekadashi brings pilgrims from across northern India.
story: After the death of the sage Jamadagni, Renuka is said to have entered these waters and become the lake itself, promising her son Parashurama an annual reunion.

name: Trilokinath Temple
deity: Avalokiteshvara to Buddhists, Shiva as Trilokinath to Hindus
builtDisplay: 7th-8th c.; marble image dated to the 12th c.
dynasty: Early medieval Himalayan; columns attributed to King Lalitaditya
style: Curvilinear stone shikhara crowned by an amalaka
significance: A hilltop shrine above the Chenab in Lahaul, worshipped by Tibetan Buddhists as Avalokiteshvara and by Hindus as Shiva. Prayer wheels stand beside a lingam, making it one of the clearest surviving examples of Himalayan religious syncretism.
story: A raja of Kullu is said to have tried to carry off the marble image but found it immovable, and a sword mark on its right leg is pointed out as proof of the failed theft.

name: Tabo Monastery
style: Mud-brick Tibetan monastic complex of nine temples, stupas and chortens
significance: The oldest continuously functioning Buddhist monastery in India and the Himalayas, founded in 996 CE during the later spread of Buddhism in Tibet. Its murals and stucco images have earned it the name 'the Ajanta of the Himalayas'.

name: Key Monastery (Kye Gompa)
builtDisplay: present fort-monastery 17th c.; foundation traced to the 11th c.
dynasty: Gelug, era of the Fifth Dalai Lama
style: Tiered fort-monastery in the Chinese-influenced 14th-century monastic manner
significance: The largest monastery in the Spiti valley, perched at about 4,166 m above the Spiti river and home to some 250 monks. It is the valley's chief training centre for lamas and holds a notable collection of thangkas and murals.

name: Kheer Bhawani Temple
style: Marble shrine over a heptagonal sacred spring
significance: Built over a spring at Tulmulla, this is the most important temple of the Kashmiri Pandit community, who offer kheer to the goddess from which the shrine takes its name. Its Jyeshtha Ashtami mela is among the largest Hindu gatherings in Kashmir after the Amarnath yatra.
story: The goddess is said to have appeared in a dream to the Srinagar yogi Krishna Pandit Taploo and directed him to the buried holy spring.

name: Avantiswami Temple
style: Kashmiri stone temple architecture: central shrine in a colonnaded courtyard with corner shrines
significance: The ruined Vishnu temple raised by King Avantivarman at his new capital on the Jhelum, one of the finest surviving examples of 9th-century Kashmiri stone architecture. Its peristyle courtyard and carved plinths document Kashmir's Hindu building tradition before the 14th century.
story: Local tradition calls the ruins Pandav Lari, the house of the Pandavas.

name: Raghunath Temple
style: Brick shikharas with gold-plated spires and Sikh-influenced domes
significance: A complex of seven shrines in the heart of Jammu, begun by the first Dogra ruler Gulab Singh and finished by his son Ranbir Singh. Besides some three hundred carved images it holds a library of over six thousand Sanskrit manuscripts, including rare Sharada-script texts.

name: Alchi Monastery
dynasty: Rinchen Zangpo era; later Gelug under Likir
style: Tibetan architecture with strong Kashmiri influence; three-storeyed Sumtseg with elaborate wood carving
significance: A riverside temple complex holding some of the oldest surviving wall paintings in Ladakh, executed in a Kashmiri idiom that has vanished almost everywhere else. It is the best preserved of the foundations attributed to the translator Rinchen Zangpo.
story: Tradition holds that of twenty-one scholars sent by the Tibetan lama-king Yeshe-O, only Rinchen Zangpo and one other survived to bring Buddhism back to the western Himalaya.

name: Thikse Monastery
deity: Gelug school; a 15 m Maitreya Buddha in the main hall
style: Twelve-storey hilltop fort-monastery in the central Tibetan manner
significance: The largest monastery in central Ladakh, rising in tiers on a hill 19 km east of Leh and often likened to the Potala Palace in Lhasa. It houses a celebrated two-storey Maitreya image, a nunnery and a large collection of Buddhist art.
story: Two crows are said to have carried off the founder's ritual offerings and set them down in order at this hill, which he read as a sign to build here.

name: Lamayuru Monastery
builtDisplay: 10th-11th c.; oldest hall from the Rinchen Zangpo period
style: Cliffside gompa; the surviving Seng-ge-sgang temple is the oldest structure
significance: One of the largest and oldest monasteries in Ladakh, set above the eroded badlands on the Srinagar-Leh highway and home to about 150 monks. It preserves meditation caves, including one associated with the Indian scholar Naropa, and hosts well-known masked dance festivals.
story: Naropa is said to have dried up the lake that once filled this valley and founded the monastery on the bed it left behind.

name: Diskit Monastery
significance: The oldest and largest monastery of the Nubra valley, founded in the 14th century and long the religious centre for its villages. Around a hundred monks live there and the gompa also runs a school for local Tibetan children.
story: A Mongol demon hostile to Buddhism is said to have been killed here yet kept returning, and his shrivelled head and hand are believed to lie inside one of the temples.

name: Spituk Monastery
deity: Gelug school (originally of the Red Hat order)
significance: A monastery on a hill about 8 km from Leh, founded in the 11th century and converted to the Gelug order in the 15th. Its name, meaning 'exemplary', recalls Rinchen Zangpo's prediction that an exemplary religious community would arise here; some hundred monks live there and a large Kali image is unveiled at the annual Gustor festival.
story: The arhat Nyimagung is said to have blessed the site before the monastery was founded.

name: Durgiana Temple
style: Gilded dome, marble causeway and silver doors, modelled on Harmandir Sahib
significance: Amritsar's principal Hindu temple, rebuilt in 1921 by Guru Harsai Mal Kapoor on a 16th-century site. It stands in the middle of a tank and deliberately echoes the plan and gilding of the nearby Golden Temple.

name: Bhagwan Valmiki Tirath Sthal (Ram Tirath)
style: Modern complex with sacred pond, circumambulatory bridge, library and museum
significance: The Ram Tirath site west of Amritsar, rebuilt in 2016 as a large memorial complex around a gold-plated image of the sage Valmiki. It is the most important pilgrimage centre of the Valmiki community in Punjab.
story: Valmiki's ashram here is said to have sheltered Sita after her exile from Ayodhya, and to be where her twin sons Lava and Kusha were born.

name: Sthaneshwar Mahadev Temple
builtDisplay: present temple by Raghunath Rao Peshwa (18th c.)
dynasty: Maratha (Peshwa); site named by Pushpabhuti of the Vardhana line
significance: The Shiva temple that gives Thanesar its name, an ancient Kurukshetra pilgrimage site whose present structure was built by Raghunath Rao Peshwa. A gurdwara beside it marks a visit by the ninth Sikh Guru, Tegh Bahadur.
story: The Pandavas and Krishna are said to have worshipped Shiva here and received his blessing for victory in the Mahabharata war.

name: Jyotisar
deity: Krishna; the sacred banyan and an old Shiva temple
significance: The Kurukshetra site traditionally identified as the place where Krishna delivered the Bhagavad Gita, centred on an ancient banyan tree. It is a principal stop on the Krishna Circuit and has been developed with a museum and monumental bronzes.
story: Beneath this banyan Krishna is said to have counselled the wavering Arjuna and revealed to him his universal form.

name: Kalkaji Mandir
significance: A Kali temple in south Delhi opposite Nehru Place whose oldest fabric dates from the Maratha period and which gives the surrounding neighbourhood its name. It fills with pilgrims at the twice-yearly Navaratri fairs.
story: Legend holds that the goddess Kalika was born on the very spot where the temple stands.

name: Jhandewalan Temple
style: Octagonal Devi shrine on a stone platform with pavilion and circumambulatory path
significance: A major Devi temple in central Delhi founded by the cloth merchant Badri Das and run since 1944 by the Badri Bhagat Jhandewalan Temple Society. It is busiest during Navaratri and is known for large-scale community kitchens.
story: Badri Das is said to have dreamt repeatedly of a buried shrine on the hill, and on digging near a spring found an old image of Vaishno Devi in a cave, over which he raised the flag that gave the temple its name.

name: Laxminarayan Temple (Birla Mandir)
style: Nagara (north Indian) style adapted with modern construction, by Sris Chandra Chatterjee
significance: The first large Hindu temple built in Delhi, raised by the industrialists Baldeo Das and Jugal Kishore Birla and inaugurated by Mahatma Gandhi. Gandhi's condition that it stay open to worshippers of all castes made it an early landmark of temple-entry reform.

name: Chhatarpur Temple (Shri Aadya Katyayani Shakti Peetham)
style: Vesara-style marble buildings with jaali screens, mixing south and north Indian elements
significance: Delhi's second-largest temple complex, founded in 1974 and spread over some 28 hectares with more than twenty shrines in three precincts. It draws its largest crowds during Navaratri.
story: Devotees tie threads to an old tree near the entrance in the belief that wishes made there are granted.

name: Yogmaya Temple
dynasty: Late Mughal era; rebuilding attributed to Hemu in earlier phases
style: Plain hall and sanctum with a truncated shikhara and dome inside a walled enclosure
significance: A small temple beside the Qutb complex in Mehrauli, held to be the only shrine of pre-sultanate origin in Delhi still in worship. It is the Hindu focus of the city's interfaith Phool Walon Ki Sair procession.
story: Yogmaya is said to have taken the place of the infant Krishna when Kansa tried to kill him, slipping from his grasp to foretell his death.

name: Hanuman Temple, Connaught Place
deity: Hanuman in his child form (Bala Hanuman)
builtDisplay: rebuilt 1724 (Jai Singh II); earlier shrine under Akbar
significance: A busy Hanuman shrine in the middle of Connaught Place, rebuilt by Jai Singh II of Amber in 1724 and claimed as one of five Delhi temples traced to Mahabharata times. Its spire is unusual in being crowned by a crescent moon rather than the customary Hindu finial.
story: Hanuman is said to have appeared to Bhima as an old monkey during the Pandavas' exile, humbling him when he could not lift the aged creature's tail.

name: Eklingji Temple
builtDisplay: present complex 15th-16th c. (Rana Kumbha, Rana Raimal); 8th-c. origin
significance: The tutelary temple of the Mewar rulers, first attributed to Bappa Rawal in the 8th century and rebuilt by Rana Kumbha and Rana Raimal after repeated destruction. The Maharanas ruled formally as the deity's regents, which made this complex the spiritual centre of the Mewar state.
story: The 15th-century Ekalinga Mahatmya credits the original shrine to Bappa Rawal, founder of the Mewar line.

name: Shrinathji Temple
builtDisplay: 1672 (Goswami Damodar Das Bairagi under Maharana Raj Singh)
style: Haveli-form temple modelled on the Nanda temple at Gokul, with a seven-flag kalasha
significance: The chief shrine of the Pushtimarg Vaishnava tradition, built in 1672 after the image of Shrinathji was carried from Govardhan to Mewar for safety from Aurangzeb. It is laid out as a household rather than a conventional temple, with kitchen, treasury and stable serving the deity.
story: Pushtimarg hagiography says Shrinathji came to Mewar to play chaupar with the princess Ajab Kunvari, who then begged him to stay rather than return to Braj.

name: Khatushyamji Temple
style: Rajasthani temple architecture in white Makrana marble
significance: One of Rajasthan's most visited shrines, in Sikar district, where the head of Barbarika is believed to be enshrined. Millions attend the Phalguna Mela, with its Nishaan Yatra procession of pilgrim banners.
story: Barbarika, grandson of Bhima, gave his head to Krishna before the Kurukshetra war and was blessed to be worshipped as Shyam in the Kali Yuga; a local ruler is said to have found the buried image after a dream.

name: Salasar Balaji
builtDisplay: mid-18th c. (268th foundation day marked in 2022)
significance: A Hanuman shrine at Salasar near Sujangarh in Churu district and one of the busiest pilgrimage centres of the Shekhawati region. Great fairs are held there in the months of Chaitra and Ashwin.
story: A farmer at Asota is said to have turned up an image of Hanuman while ploughing and offered it the bajra churma his wife had brought; that night both the local landlord and a devotee named Mohandas dreamt they should enshrine it at Salasar.

name: Mehandipur Balaji Temple
significance: A Hanuman temple in Dausa district known throughout India for its rituals of healing and exorcism, which draw pilgrims seeking relief from affliction believed to be caused by spirits.
story: Hanuman is said to have appeared here in his Balaji form thousands of years ago.

name: Ramdevra Temple
significance: A temple raised in 1931 over the samadhi of Baba Ramdevji, the Tanwar Rajput saint who founded the village. Its annual fair in the monsoon months draws devotees from several states without distinction of caste or creed.
story: Baba Ramdevji is said to have taken samadhi in 1459 at the age of thirty-three, having founded the settlement and dug the Ram Sarovar tank.

name: Galtaji
deity: Several shrines; the hilltop temple is dedicated to Surya
builtDisplay: from the early 15th c.; Sun Temple under Sawai Jai Singh II
dynasty: Ramanandi sampradaya under Amber and Jaipur patronage
style: Rajasthani and Mughal blend, with rounded pavilion roofs, carved pillars and frescoes
significance: A pilgrimage site in a ravine about 10 km east of Jaipur where temples are built around natural springs feeding a chain of sacred tanks. Long a leading centre of the Ramanandi Vaishnavas, it fills with bathers at Makar Sankranti.
story: The place takes its name from the sage Galav, said to have performed his penance here.

name: Govind Dev Ji Temple
deity: Radha and Krishna as Govind Dev Ji
style: Temple within the City Palace; its Satsang Hall spans 119 ft of unsupported concrete roof
significance: Jaipur's principal Krishna temple, set in the City Palace complex around images that Sawai Jai Singh II brought from Vrindavan. It is also where Baladeva Vidyabhushana composed the Govinda Bhashya, a foundational Gaudiya Vaishnava commentary.
story: The image is said to have been made by Bajranabh, Krishna's great-grandson, as one of three portraying his feet, chest and face.

name: Moti Dungri Ganesh Temple
dynasty: Kachhwaha of Jaipur, under Madho Singh I
style: Nagara-style temple below a hill palace with Scottish castle detailing, in limestone and marble
significance: A Ganesha temple below the Moti Dungri hill in Jaipur, built in 1761 and now visited by well over a hundred thousand devotees a year. It stands close to the city's Birla Mandir and is one of Jaipur's most popular shrines.
story: The sindoor-coloured image is held to be more than five hundred years old, brought from Gujarat to Udaipur and then carried to Jaipur in 1761.

name: Birla Mandir, Jaipur
significance: A white marble temple in Jaipur's Tilak Nagar built by the B. M. Birla Foundation and opened in 1988. Its outer walls are unusual in carrying figures from other traditions, including Christ, the Buddha, Confucius and Socrates, alongside Hindu deities.
story: Tradition has it that a Maharaja sold the Birla family the land for the temple for a single rupee.

name: Shila Devi Temple
deity: Durga in her form as Shila Devi
significance: A Shakti shrine inside Amer Fort near Jaipur, established in 1604 by Raja Man Singh I, with carved pillars and an image cut from a black stone slab. It is a major centre of worship during Navratri and part of a UNESCO World Heritage site.
story: Man Singh I is said to have been divinely instructed to retrieve the goddess from the sea at Jessore, and the image was carved from the stone slab, or shila, that he recovered.

name: Jeen Mata Temple
deity: Jeen Mata (Jayanti Mata), a form of Shakti
significance: A hilltop Shakti shrine in the Shekhawati region of Sikar district, built of marble and limestone, which Wikipedia dates by tradition to around the 8th century. An eternal flame is said to have been kept burning at the shrine for centuries.
story: When soldiers of Aurangzeb's time approached the hill a swarm of bees is said to have driven them off, after which the goddess became known as Bhanwaron ki Devi, the goddess of the bees.

name: Rani Sati Temple
deity: Rani Sati, also called Narayani Devi
style: White marble with murals and glass mosaics
significance: The largest temple in India dedicated to Rani Sati, a Rajasthani woman said to have lived between the 13th and 17th centuries. It is built of white marble and decorated with wall paintings, murals and glass mosaic work.
story: Tradition holds that Rani Sati was a rebirth of Narayani Devi, who avenged her husband Tandhan's killing by a king before immolating herself on his pyre.

name: Sachiya Mata Temple
deity: Sachiya Mata, also called Shri Osiya Mataji
significance: A goddess temple at Osian in Jodhpur district, as old and as important as the neighbouring Mahavira Jain temple and carrying decorative features of Jain workmanship. She is honoured as the protective deity of the Oswal community.
story: Jain tradition says the teacher Ratnaprabhasuri turned the fierce goddess Chamunda into the vegetarian deity Sachiya Mata, who then became guardian of the Oswals.

name: Kaila Devi Temple
deity: Kaila Devi, worshipped as Mahalakshmi and Mahayogini
significance: A marble Shakti temple in the hills of Karauli district, founded by Maharaja Gopal Singh of the Jadaun house and completed in 1730. It draws large crowds to its annual Kaila Devi fair.
story: A yogi's bullock cart carrying the goddess's image is said to have halted in the forested hills, and by divine ordinance the image was installed at that very spot.

name: Sanwaliyaji Temple
significance: A Krishna temple at Mandphiya in Chittorgarh district, regarded as second only to Shrinathji at Nathdwara among Vaishnava pilgrimage sites in the region and drawing devotees from Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat.
story: In 1840 a cowherd named Bholaram is said to have dreamt of three divine images buried at Bagund village; the three that were unearthed were enshrined at three nearby sites, of which Mandphiya became the principal shrine.

name: Charbhuja Temple, Garhbor
style: Shikhara temple with a tall spire over the sanctum
significance: A Krishna temple at Garhbor in the Kumbhalgarh tehsil of Rajsamand district, about 32 km from Kumbhalgarh, whose 85 cm four-armed image holds conch, discus, mace and lotus. Its main observances are Fagotsav, Janmashtami and Annakut.

name: Sahasra Bahu Temples (Sas-Bahu), Nagda
deity: Vishnu (Sahasra Bahu, 'one with a thousand arms')
significance: A pair of ruined stone temples at Nagda, an early capital of Mewar near Udaipur, lavishly carved inside and now protected by the Archaeological Survey of India. Their local name Sas-Bahu is a corruption of Sahasra Bahu.

name: Harshat Mata Temple
significance: A ruined early-medieval temple beside the Chand Baori stepwell at Abhaneri, laid out in panchayatana plan with a main shrine and four subsidiary shrines. Art historians debate whether it was originally a Vaishnava or a Durga shrine before becoming the shrine of Harshat Mata.

name: Neelkanth Temple, Alwar
significance: A hill temple in an isolated valley beside Sariska National Park in Alwar district, built by the local Pratihara feudatory Parmeshwara Mathanadeva. Its sculpture, including erotic panels, is compared to the work at Khajuraho.

name: Tanot Mata Temple
deity: Tanot Mata (Aavad Mata), regarded as a form of Hinglaj Mata
significance: A desert shrine in Jaisalmer district close to the Pakistan border, founded in 828 CE by the Bhati Rajput king Tanu Rao and now also serving as a war memorial cared for by border troops.
story: During the 1965 war some three thousand shells are said to have fallen on the temple without exploding, and the 1971 victory at nearby Longewala is locally credited to the goddess's protection.

name: Kapil Muni Temple, Kolayat
significance: A pilgrimage town in Bikaner district built around a desert lake ringed by 52 bathing ghats, marble temples and sandstone pavilions, centred on the sage Kapila. Its Kartik fair draws thousands of pilgrims and doubles as a camel market.
story: Kapila is believed to have shed his body here beneath a peepal tree, and bathers hold that the lake washes away sin.

name: Bhandasar Jain Temple
style: Red sandstone, five-ratha sanctum with shikhara
significance: A three-storey Svetambara Jain temple in Bikaner built in red sandstone with yellow-stone carving, famous for its frescoes, leaf paintings and mirror work depicting the lives of the twenty-four Tirthankaras. It is a protected monument of the Archaeological Survey of India.
story: Local tradition claims that forty thousand kilograms of ghee were used instead of water in mixing the mortar for the temple.

name: Kiradu Temples
deity: Shiva (the best-preserved Someshvara temple); a Vishnu temple also stands at the site
significance: A group of five ruined Hindu temples in the Thar Desert near Barmer, built by vassals of the Chalukya monarchs and richly carved with animal and human figures. An inscription of 1178 CE records repairs to a temple damaged during Ghurid raids.

name: Chandrabadani Devi Temple
deity: Sati, worshipped through a Shri Yantra carved on stone
significance: A Siddhpeeth on a Garhwal Himalayan ridge at about 2,277 m in Tehri district, where the goddess is worshipped not as an image but as a Shri Yantra carved into a flat stone. An annual fair is held in April.
story: The site is held to be where the torso of Sati fell as Shiva carried her body, her weapons scattering across the hill, which iron tridents at the shrine are said to recall.

name: Purnagiri Temple
deity: Maa Purnagiri, a form of Sati
significance: A Shakti Peeth on a hill near Tanakpur in Champawat district, at about 910 m, drawing thousands of pilgrims each year, above all during Chaitra Navratri in March and April.
story: The shrine is held to mark the spot where the navel of Sati fell as Shiva carried her body across the world.

name: Baleshwar Temple
significance: A stone temple complex at Champawat, an early capital of the Chand dynasty, renowned for its carving and accompanied by shrines to Ratneshwar and Champawati Durga. A copperplate inscription records the reconstruction being completed by Hari Chand in 1423.

name: Kasar Devi Temple
deity: Kasar Devi, a form of Durga
builtDisplay: rebuilt 1948; shrine traced to 2nd c. CE
significance: A ridge-top shrine near Almora set among huge rock formations, with a cave-like sanctum, an eternal flame and a continuously burning dhuni. The present structure was built in 1948, and the site drew Swami Vivekananda in the 1890s and later became a landmark of the Hippie trail.

name: Mukteshwar Dham Temple
significance: A Shiva temple on the highest point of Mukteshwar in Nainital district, from which the hill town takes its name. The cliffs beside it, known locally as Chauli-ki-Jali, are a well-known viewpoint.

name: Gurdwara Paonta Sahib
deity: Dedicated to Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru
significance: A gurdwara on the bank of the Yamuna founded by Guru Gobind Singh in 1685, where he stayed some four and a half years, longer than anywhere else, and composed a large body of writing. It is also the birthplace of his eldest son, Sahibzada Ajit Singh.
story: The name comes from paon, foot, and tika, became stable, recalling that the Guru's horse halted at this spot.

name: Gurudwara Manikaran Sahib
deity: Associated with Guru Nanak, the first Sikh Guru
significance: A gurdwara in the Parvati valley of Kullu district, standing beside hot springs that Sikh tradition connects with Guru Nanak's visit during his third udasi. The spring water is used to cook langar and the site is revered by Sikhs and Hindus alike.
story: Sikh tradition holds that Guru Nanak caused the hot springs to appear so that food could be cooked for the community kitchen.

name: Ranchhodrai Temple, Dakor
deity: Ranchhodrai, the Trivikrama form of Vishnu, identified with Krishna
significance: A major Krishna pilgrimage temple in Kheda district, built between 1769 and 1772 by the Pune Brahmin Gopal Tambvekar, with four gold-capped shikharas and seven domes inside fort-like walls beside the Gomti lake. It is a leading centre of Pushtimarg Vaishnava worship in Gujarat.
story: Devotees hold that the image was miraculously carried from Dwarka to Dakor by the devotee Bodana in 1151.

name: Shamlaji Temple
deity: Shamlaji, Vishnu in his Trivikrama form, also called Gadadhara Vishnu
significance: A major Vaishnava pilgrimage centre on the Meshwo river in Aravalli district. The site was already an important religious centre in the sixth century and probably housed a sculpture workshop whose work travelled far across western India; the present temple dates from the 15th-16th centuries.

name: Bahucharaji Temple
significance: A major Shakti pilgrimage centre in Mehsana district that gives the town of Becharaji its name, now managed by the state government and equipped with guesthouses and dharamshalas for pilgrims. Its great fair falls on the full moon of Chaitra.

name: Chamunda Mata Temple, Chotila
significance: A hilltop shrine to Chamunda on Chotila hill in Surendranagar district, reached by a climb of some 920 steps and one of the busiest Shakti shrines in Saurashtra.

name: Jalaram Temple, Virpur
deity: The saint Jalaram Bapa, together with the images of Rama, Sita, Lakshman and Hanuman he worshipped
builtDisplay: shrine at the saint's house, 19th c.
significance: A shrine in the house complex at Virpur where the saint Jalaram Bapa (1799-1881) lived, preserving his belongings and the images he worshipped. It is unusual among Indian temples in having refused all offerings since 9 February 2000, and draws crowds at Jalaram Jayanti.
story: The temple displays the jholi and danda that Jalaram is said to have received from God himself.

name: Akshardham, Gandhinagar
style: Traditional Hindu temple architecture in pink Rajasthan sandstone, designed by Chandrakant Sompura
significance: A 23-acre BAPS Swaminarayan complex in Gandhinagar built without steel or iron, from 6,000 tonnes of pink sandstone, with 97 carved pillars, 17 domes and 264 sculpted figures around a gold-leafed image of Swaminarayan. It also houses exhibition halls, gardens and a water show.

name: Nishkalank Mahadev Temple
significance: A Shiva shrine standing out in the Arabian Sea off Koliyak in Bhavnagar district, reachable on foot only at low tide and submerged when the tide returns. Maha Shivratri and Navaratri draw large numbers of pilgrims.
story: The Pandavas are said to have installed five Shivalingas here on Krishna's instruction to expiate the sins of the Mahabharata war.

name: Koteshwar Temple
deity: Shiva, as a four-foot self-manifested lingam; also called Kotilingeshwar
style: Stone temple with three domes in the porch and a black marble shrine
significance: An ancient Shiva site near the mouth of Kori Creek at the western edge of Kutch, some 178 km from Bhuj and 4 km from Narayan Sarovar. The present structure dates from 1820, and the site was noted by the seventh-century Chinese traveller Xuanzang.
story: Ravana is said to have been given the lingam by Shiva and to have dropped it here, whereupon it multiplied so that the original could not be told apart, giving the place its name of ten million gods.

name: Narayan Sarovar
deity: Trikamray (Vishnu), with shrines to Lakshminarayan, Adinarayan, Govardhannath, Dwarkanath, Lakshmiji and Kalyanray
style: Domed temples in the manner of the Dwarka shrines
significance: One of the five sacred lakes of Hinduism, the Panch-Sarovar, in Lakhpat taluka of Kutch. Its main temples were built in 1734 by Vagheli Mahakunvar, wife of Rao Deshalji I, with the Kalyanray temple added in 1828.
story: The Saraswati river is said to have reached the sea near this spot, which is what made the lake holy.

name: Mata no Madh (Ashapura Mata Temple)
deity: Ashapura Mata, patron goddess of Kutch
significance: The shrine of Ashapura Mata, household deity of the Jadeja rulers and patron goddess of Kutch, first built in the 14th century by the ministers Ajo and Anagor and rebuilt in 1823 after the 1819 earthquake. Thousands come during Navaratri.
story: Soldiers of Mian Ghulam Shah Kalhoro are said to have been struck blind when they attacked the temple in 1762, and their ruler donated a great bell when their sight returned.

name: Rukmini Devi Temple
deity: Rukmini, chief queen of Krishna and an incarnation of Lakshmi
style: Richly carved, with narathara and gajathara panels at the base of the tower
significance: A carved temple about 2 km outside Dwarka housing a marble image of Rukmini holding conch, discus, mace and lotus. Local custom holds that a pilgrimage to Dwarka is complete only after worshipping here.
story: The Skanda Purana explains the temple's distance from Krishna's own shrine by the curse of the sage Durvasa, who condemned the couple to live apart for twelve years after Rukmini offered water to Krishna before him.

name: Hutheesing Jain Temple
significance: A white marble Jain temple in Ahmedabad built in 1848, begun by Hutheesing Kesarisinh and completed under his widow Harkunwar, with 52 subsidiary shrines around the main temple and a 78-foot Manastambha added for Mahavira's 2500th birth anniversary. It was raised during a severe famine and employed hundreds of artisans for two years.

name: Taranga Jain Temple
style: Maru-Gurjara, with bhumija and sekhari elements in the shikhara
significance: A hill tirtha in Mehsana district whose main temple, built in 1161 by the Solanki king Kumarapala under the guidance of Acharya Hemachandra, holds a 2.75 m white marble image of Ajitnatha. The site has separate Svetambara and Digambara compounds with nineteen temples between them.
story: The name is locally traced to a shrine of the goddess Tara said to have been built by an ancient Buddhist king.

name: Girnar Jain Temples
builtDisplay: main temple rebuilt 1129 (Sajjana, under Jayasimha Siddharaja)
significance: A cluster of Jain temples on Mount Girnar in Junagadh district, built in grey granite with marble carving. The Neminath temple was rebuilt in 1129 by Sajjana, governor under Jayasimha Siddharaja, the Ambika temple predates 784 CE, and further shrines were added by merchant patrons in the 15th century. The site is one of the Svetambara Pancha Tirth.
story: Neminath is said to have renounced the world after seeing animals penned for slaughter at his own wedding feast, and to have attained omniscience and moksha from Girnar's highest peak.

name: Kayavarohan Temple (Lakulish)
deity: Shiva in the form of Lakulisha, as a black stone lingam
dynasty: Modern restoration on an ancient site
significance: A Shaiva centre at Karvan in Vadodara district, regarded as the birthplace of Lakulisha, the second-century revivalist of the Pashupata school, and counted among the sixty-eight Shiva pilgrimage sites. Its lingam bears the image of a meditating yogi holding parchments and a citron, and the temples were restored in the late twentieth century by Kripalvanand.
story: The name is read as kaya, body, plus avarohan, descent: the place where the Lord's body descended.

name: Gop Temple
deity: Surya, the sun god, with Vaishnava, Skanda and Shaiva imagery also present
style: Unusual variant of the Nagara style, with a square plan, pyramidal shikhara and corbelled construction
significance: Standing on the Vartu river in Jamnagar district, this is one of the earliest surviving stone temples in Gujarat and the earliest in Saurashtra, radiocarbon-dated to about 550 CE. It is a Monument of National Importance.

name: Shankheshwar Parshwanath Jain Temple
significance: A leading Jain pilgrimage centre in Patan district. The present Parshwanath temple was built in 1811, but Jain temples are recorded at Shankheshwar from at least 1155 CE, and ruins of an older temple dated 1596 stand nearby.

name: Aundha Nagnath Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Aundha in Hingoli district, Marathwada, counted as the eighth of the twelve Jyotirlingas.

name: Shri Vaijnath Temple (Vaidyanath Jyotirlinga)
significance: A Shiva temple at Parli Vaijnath in Beed district counted as the fifth of the twelve Jyotirlingas, and among the most visited pilgrimage shrines of Marathwada.

name: Tulja Bhavani Temple
significance: A 12th-century temple to the goddess Bhavani, counted among the Shakta pithas and one of the three-and-a-half principal Shakti seats of Maharashtra. It is among the most heavily visited pilgrimage shrines in the state.
story: The Skanda Purana relates that the goddess came to the aid of the ascetic widow Anubhuti on Yamunachala hill and afterwards settled at Tuljapur as Tulja Bhavani.

name: Mahalakshmi Temple, Kolhapur
significance: A major goddess temple where Mahalakshmi is worshipped locally as Ambabai, reckoned one of the three-and-a-half Shakti seats of the Shakta tradition in Maharashtra.
story: The goddess is said to have manifested here to destroy the demon Kolhasur, from whom Kolhapur takes its name.

name: Renuka Devi Temple, Mahur
significance: A hill shrine to Renuka, mother of Parashurama, counted among the three-and-a-half Shakta pithas of Maharashtra; the surrounding town is also revered as the birthplace of Dattatreya.
story: Renuka was mortally wounded by Sahasrarjuna when she refused to surrender the cow Kamadhenu, and her son Parashurama performed her last rites at Mahur, where she then manifested on the hill.

name: Saptashrungi Temple
deity: Goddess Saptashrungi Nivasini (a form of Durga)
significance: A hill shrine where the goddess is carved into a cave in a sheer rock face, counted among Maharashtra's three-and-a-half Shakta pithas and among the wider set of 51 Shakta pithas.
story: The right arm of Sati is said to have fallen here as Shiva carried her body across the world.

name: Shani Shingnapur Temple
deity: Shani, worshipped as a swayambhu black stone
significance: An open-air shrine to Shani built around a self-manifested black stone. The surrounding village is known for houses and shops built without doors or locks, in the belief that the god himself punishes theft.
story: Shepherds are said to have struck a black stone that bled, after which Shani appeared in a shepherd's dream, claimed the stone as his own and promised the village protection from theft.

name: Khandoba Temple, Jejuri
deity: Khandoba (Malhari Martand, a form of Shiva)
significance: One of the foremost pilgrimage centres of Maharashtra, this hilltop temple to Khandoba is the family deity shrine of farming, Brahmin and Dhangar communities across the Deccan.
story: Khandoba is said to have descended as an avatar of Shiva to subdue the demon brothers Mani and Malla, killing one and pardoning the other when he vowed to serve people.

name: Bhuleshwar Temple
significance: A hilltop Shiva temple about 45 km from Pune, protected as a monument and known for its dense figural stone carving worked in black basalt.
story: Devotees say that sweets offered before the linga sometimes disappear from the offering bowl.

name: Dagadusheth Halwai Ganapati Temple
significance: Pune's best-known Ganesha temple, visited by well over a hundred thousand devotees a year and the focus of a prominent ten-day Ganeshotsav celebration.
story: The sweet-seller Dagadusheth Halwai and his wife Laxmibai are said to have founded the shrine on a sage's advice after losing their only son in a plague.

name: Chintamani Temple, Theur
significance: One of the larger and better-known Ashtavinayaka shrines, about 25 km from Pune near the confluence of the Bhima and Mula-Mutha. It was a major Ganapatya centre that drew royal patronage under the Peshwa Madhavrao I.
story: Ganesha is said to have recovered the wish-granting Chintamani jewel from the greedy king Gana for the sage Kapila and then stayed on at Theur.

name: Mayureshwar (Moreshwar) Temple, Morgaon
builtDisplay: not earlier than 17th c.; Peshwa-era patronage
significance: The starting and finishing point of the eight-temple Ashtavinayaka pilgrimage and the principal centre of the Ganapatya sect, enclosed by a tall stone wall with minarets at its corners.
story: Ganesha is said to have incarnated as Mayuresvara, riding a peacock, to defeat the demon Sindhu.

name: Siddhivinayak Temple, Siddhatek
style: black stone, north-facing sanctum under a domed ceiling
significance: The third of the eight Ashtavinayaka shrines and the only one in the Ahilyanagar (Ahmednagar) district; its image is unusual in having a right-turned trunk.
story: Vishnu is said to have performed penance here invoking Ganesha, receiving the siddhis with which he overcame the demons Madhu and Kaitabha.

name: Ballaleshwar Temple, Pali
style: east-facing stone temple laid out in the shape of the letter 'shri'
significance: One of the eight Ashtavinayaka shrines and the only Ganesha temple known by the name of a devotee rather than of the god.
story: A boy named Ballal worshipped a stone as Ganesha despite his father's beatings; the god appeared, healed him and agreed to remain there under the boy's name.

name: Varadvinayak Temple, Mahad
significance: One of the eight Ashtavinayaka shrines, in Mahad village of Khalapur taluka; the present temple was raised in 1725 by the Peshwa general Ramji Mahadev Biwalkar around an image reported found in 1690.
story: The sage Gritsamada's prayers are said to have won Ganesha's promise to dwell here permanently as Varadavinayaka, the granter of boons.

name: Girijatmaj Temple, Lenyadri
builtDisplay: 1st–3rd c. Buddhist cave, later given to Ganesha worship
style: rock-cut Buddhist vihara adapted as a Hindu shrine
significance: The only Ashtavinayaka shrine set on a mountain and inside a Buddhist cave group, occupying cells of Cave 7 of the Lenyadri excavations.
story: Parvati is said to have meditated here for twelve years, after which Ganesha granted that he would be born as her son.

name: Vigneshwara (Vighnahar) Temple, Ozar
deity: Ganesha as Vigneshwara, remover of obstacles
style: walled courtyard temple with a gold-foiled shikhara and lamp towers
significance: One of the eight Ashtavinayaka shrines, believed to house a self-existent image; it was renovated by Chimaji Appa after his capture of Vasai Fort and again in 1967.
story: Ganesha subdued the demon Vignasura, sent by Indra to wreck a king's sacrifice, and at the demon's request took the title Vigneshwara.

name: Mahaganapati Temple, Ranjangaon
significance: An east-facing Ashtavinayaka shrine whose main structure dates from the Peshwa period and was later renovated by Madhavrao I and Sardar Kibe of Indore.
story: The presiding image, gifted by the local Khollam family of goldsmiths, is described as having ten trunks and twenty arms.

name: Mumba Devi Temple
deity: Goddess Mumba, a local form of the mother goddess
builtDisplay: rebuilt at Bhuleshwar after 1739–1770; shrine about six centuries old
significance: The temple of the goddess from whom Mumbai takes its name, first built by Koli fishermen at Bori Bunder and re-established at Bhuleshwar after the original was destroyed in the mid-18th century.
story: Parvati is said to have taken birth as the fisherwoman Mumba among the Koli people, and to have stayed on as their village deity at their request.

name: Mahalakshmi Temple, Mumbai
significance: One of Mumbai's most visited temples, built in 1831 by the merchant Dhakji Dadaji and housing the three goddesses of the Tridevi.

name: Walkeshwar Temple
significance: An old Shiva temple on Malabar Hill in South Mumbai, associated with the adjoining Banganga freshwater tank and used as a venue for Hindustani classical music festivals.
story: Rama is said to have paused here on his way to Lanka, fashioning a linga of sand and shooting an arrow into the ground to bring up the Ganga as the Banganga tank.

name: Kanheri Caves
deity: Buddhist monastic complex of viharas and chaityas
significance: A group of 109 caves cut into a basalt outcrop inside Sanjay Gandhi National Park, forming a long-lived Buddhist monastic and teaching centre on the Konkan coast with elaborate water-management works.

name: Karla Caves
builtDisplay: 2nd c. BCE–5th c. CE; Great Chaitya c. 50–70 CE
style: rock-cut chaitya hall with apsidal plan and wooden roof ribs
significance: A rock-cut Buddhist cave complex near Lonavala containing the Great Chaitya, the largest rock-cut chaitya hall in India, funded by rulers, merchants and Yavana donors.

name: Bhaja Caves
builtDisplay: 2nd c. BCE, with inscriptions to the 2nd c. CE
style: rock-cut Buddhist architecture imitating timber construction
significance: A group of 22 rock-cut caves near Lonavala whose barrel-vaulted chaitya and reliefs document the early development of Buddhist architecture; one carving is cited as evidence that drums of the tabla type were in use over two millennia ago.

name: Global Vipassana Pagoda
deity: Vipassana meditation dome dedicated to the teaching of Sayagyi U Ba Khin
style: Burmese, modelled on the Shwedagon Pagoda
significance: A donation-funded meditation hall at Gorai seating roughly 8,000 practitioners beneath what is described as the world's largest stone dome built without supporting pillars; it was inaugurated in 2009 as a monument to Vipassana practice.

name: Deekshabhoomi
style: modelled on the Great Stupa at Sanchi
significance: The Nagpur site where B. R. Ambedkar and some 400,000 followers embraced Buddhism on 14 October 1956, the largest mass religious conversion on record; its hollow stupa is central to Ambedkarite Buddhism and draws millions of pilgrims.

name: Ganpatipule Temple
significance: A shrine on the Konkan shore in Ratnagiri district whose west-facing image, said to have risen from the soil, makes it one of coastal Maharashtra's busiest pilgrimage and tourist destinations.
story: Local tradition holds that Ganpati moved here from nearby Gule after taking offence at a villager's remark, the name Pule meaning that he came forward.

name: Shiv Mandir, Ambarnath (Ambreshwar Temple)
significance: An 11th-century Shilahara temple on the Waldhuni river near Mumbai, likely raised by King Chhittaraja. It is a well-known example of Bhumija architecture, with a sanctum set below floor level and a shikhara left unfinished.

name: Kopeshwar Temple
significance: A 12th-century Shiva temple on the bank of the Krishna, built under the Shilahara king Gandaraditya and known for its open Swargamandapa and dense carving; it is noted as a Shiva temple that also enshrines an image of Vishnu.
story: Vishnu is said to have brought Shiva here to calm his rage after Sati's death at Daksha's sacrifice, which is why the god is called Kopeshwar, the wrathful one.

name: Shri Gajanan Maharaj Sansthan, Shegaon
deity: Samadhi shrine of Sant Gajanan Maharaj
significance: The samadhi temple of the saint Gajanan Maharaj, who died in 1910, administered by a trust formed in 1908. It has made Shegaon one of the largest pilgrimage centres of Vidarbha, drawing hundreds of thousands of visitors a year.
story: A dhuni fire lit by the saint is said to have burned continuously beside his samadhi ever since.

name: Shree Swami Samarth Math, Akkalkot
deity: Samadhi shrine of Swami Samarth of Akkalkot
significance: The shrine of Swami Samarth, a 19th-century master of the Dattatreya tradition who came to Akkalkot around 1856 and took samadhi in 1878; his large following across Maharashtra keeps the ashram a busy pilgrimage centre.
story: The Swami said that he had emerged from a banyan tree and had earlier borne the name Nrusimha Bhan, and devotees regard him as an incarnation of Dattatreya.

name: Mangueshi Temple
deity: Shiva as Manguesh, worshipped as a linga
builtDisplay: linga moved here 1560; present structure Maratha era, renovated 1890 and 1973
style: Goan Saraswat, with a seven-storey deepastambha
significance: One of the largest and most visited temples in Goa and the family deity shrine of many Gaud Saraswat Brahmins; the linga was carried here from Kushasthali in 1560 to escape Portuguese conversions.
story: Shiva is said to have fled Kailash after losing at dice and to have taken the form of a tiger to frighten Parvati, whose cry of Mam Girisha became the name Manguesh.

name: Shanta Durga Temple
style: Goan Saraswat, with pyramidal shikhara and a balustraded dome
significance: A Goud Saraswat Brahmin temple about 30 km from Panaji, patronised by Baji Rao I in 1738 and serving as the family deity shrine for many Saraswat households.
story: Shantadurga is said to have stepped between Shiva and Vishnu in a destructive quarrel, holding one on each hand until peace was restored.

name: Mahalasa Narayani Temple, Mardol
deity: Mahalasa Narayani, a form of Vishnu as Mohini
significance: The chief temple of Mahalasa, a major pilgrimage centre in Ponda taluka and the family goddess shrine of Gaud Saraswat and Daivajnya Brahmin and Vaishnava households across Goa and the Konkan.
story: Folk tradition makes Mhalsa the daughter of the merchant Timmaseth, married to Khandoba at his command in a dream, at which two Shiva lingas are said to have appeared.

name: Mahadev Temple, Tambdi Surla
significance: A 13th-century basalt temple deep in the forest of the Western Ghats, protected as a Monument of National Importance and the only well-preserved example of Kadamba temple architecture surviving in Goa.
story: Local tradition holds that a large king cobra lives permanently in the dim sanctum beside the linga.

name: Saptakoteshwar Temple
style: Kadamba plan with a shallow Mughal-style dome, European-style mandapa and a deepastamba
significance: One of the six great Shiva sites of the Konkan and the family deity shrine of the Kadamba kings; the present structure was commissioned by Shivaji in 1668 after the linga had been rescued and moved during Portuguese rule.
story: The Skanda Purana relates that seven sages made a linga of seven metals here, and that Shiva agreed to remain as Saptakoteshwar, lord of the seven.

name: Bhojeshwar Temple
significance: An unfinished 11th-century Shiva temple attributed to the Paramara king Bhoja, housing a 7.5-foot linga. Because work stopped, the site preserves architectural drawings, mason marks and quarry remains that document medieval temple construction in unusual detail.
story: Merutunga's Prabandha-Chintamani has King Bhoja describing to the poet Magha the Bhojasvamin temple he intended to raise in Malwa, though the two men lived centuries apart.

name: Sharda Devi Temple, Maihar
significance: A hilltop temple on Trikut hill counted among the Shakti Pithas and one of the busiest goddess shrines of Madhya Pradesh, especially during Navaratri.
story: Sati's necklace is said to have fallen here, giving Maihar its name, and the warriors Alha and Udal are remembered as the first to worship the goddess in the forest.

name: Pitambara Peeth
deity: Goddess Bagalamukhi, one of the ten Mahavidyas
significance: A temple complex and ashram at Datia founded in the 1920s by Shree Swami Ji, among the best known shrines of Bagalamukhi, with further temples to Dhumavati, Parashurama, Hanuman and Kal Bhairav and a Sanskrit library.
story: The Vankhandeswar linga within the complex is held by tradition to date from the time of the Mahabharata.

name: Bijasan Mata Temple, Salkanpur
deity: Bijasan Devi (Vindhyavasini, a form of Durga)
significance: A Siddhapeeth of Vindhyavasini Bijasan Devi standing about 800 feet above the plain near Rehti in Sehore district, and one of the most frequented goddess shrines in Madhya Pradesh.

name: Ram Raja Temple
deity: Rama, worshipped as a reigning king
significance: The only temple where Rama is worshipped as a king, and in a palace rather than a purpose-built shrine; it was established by Madhukar Shah of Orchha and his queen and receives hundreds of thousands of visitors a year.
story: Queen Ganesh Kunwari is said to have received the child Rama in her lap at the Sarayu in Ayodhya and to have brought him to Orchha on three conditions, after which the image refused to be moved from her palace.

name: Chaturbhuj Temple, Orchha
deity: Vishnu; intended for Rama and now serving Radha Krishna
style: Nagara with Maru-Gurjara elements, combining temple, fort and palace forms
significance: A towering Bundela temple at Orchha with one of the tallest vimanas of any Indian temple, begun by Madhukar Shah and completed by his son Vir Singh Deo during Akbar's reign.
story: It was raised for the Rama image the queen brought from Ayodhya, but the image would not be moved from her palace, which became the Ram Raja temple instead.

name: Chausath Yogini Temple, Mitaoli
deity: The 64 Yoginis, with Shiva in the central shrine
style: circular hypaethral yogini temple with 65 chambers
significance: An 11th-century circular yogini temple, also called the Ekattarso Mahadeva temple, built under King Devapala and protected by the ASI; its ring plan is often cited as an inspiration for the design of India's parliament building.
story: The yoginis were believed able to fly, which is given as the reason the central courtyard is left open to the sky.

name: Bateshwar Hindu Temples
style: post-Gupta and early Gurjara-Pratihara North Indian, including mandapika shrines
significance: A group of nearly 200 sandstone temples and ruins spread over about 25 acres north of Gwalior, forming an unusually dense record of experimentation in early medieval temple design in central India.

name: Kakanmath Temple
style: North Indian, with a shikhara about 30 m high
significance: A ruined 11th-century Shiva temple at Sihoniya commissioned by the Kachchhapaghata ruler Kirttiraja, now a Monument of National Importance under the ASI.
story: The name is popularly explained as honouring Kakanavati, said to have been the queen of one Surajpala.

name: Udayagiri Caves
deity: Vishnu and Shiva, with one cave dedicated to the Jain tirthankara Parshvanatha
builtDisplay: early 3rd–5th c.; principal caves consecrated 401 CE
significance: A hillside of rock-cut sanctuaries near Vidisha holding some of the oldest surviving Hindu temple architecture and iconography in India, including the great Varaha panel, and the only Gupta site with securely dated royal inscriptions.
story: The Varaha panel shows Vishnu in boar form lifting the earth goddess Bhudevi clear of the demon Hiranyaksha.

name: Chausath Yogini Temple, Bhedaghat (Golaki Math)
deity: Eighty-one yoginis around a central Shiva-Bhairava shrine
style: circular yogini temple about 125 ft across with 81 cells
significance: The largest of the circular yogini temples, set on a hilltop above the Narmada near Jabalpur and built under Yuvaraja II of the Kalachuris; unusually it holds 81 shrine cells rather than the customary 64.

name: Narmada Udgam Temple, Amarkantak
significance: The principal temple of the pilgrim town of Amarkantak, enclosing the kund accepted as the source of the Narmada. It was raised by the Kalachuris of Tripuri and later renovated by the Holkar queen Ahilyabai.
story: Adi Shankaracharya is said to have declared this stream the true source of the Narmada while searching for its origin.

name: Ahilyeshwar Temple and Maheshwar Ghats
significance: Maheshwar was the Narmada-bank capital of the Holkar queen Ahilyabai, who endowed the town with temples, a fort-palace and the broad stone ghats that still define its riverfront.

name: Kundalpur Jain Temples
style: Square shrines with domed roofs and pinnacles
significance: A Digambar Jain pilgrimage complex of roughly fifty temples on and around a hill northeast of Damoh, centred on the colossal Rishabhanatha image known as Bade Baba. The shrine was renovated around 1700 with help from the Bundela ruler Chhatrasal.
story: Jain tradition holds that Shridhar Kevali, the last of the omniscient ones, attained liberation here.

name: Bawangaja
style: Monolithic Kayotsarga colossus in brown stone
significance: A Digambar Jain pilgrimage centre in the Satpura range of south-western Madhya Pradesh whose 84-foot rock-cut standing image of Rishabhadeva is among the largest monolithic Jain statues in the world, set among a group of eleven temples.
story: Indrajit, Kumbhakarna and other ascetics are said to have attained emancipation here through self-meditation, and their ancient footprint images are preserved at the Chulgiri shrine.

name: Maladevi Temple, Gyaraspur
significance: The largest and finest surviving temple at Gyaraspur, cut partly into the hillside and dedicated to Adinatha, with a dense sculptural programme of tirthankaras, yakshas and yakshis and a foundation inscription of the reign of Valleka.

name: Pashupatinath Temple, Mandsaur
style: Western school of early Indian art
significance: A Shiva temple at Mandsaur, ancient Dashapura, housing a rare 4.5 m eight-faced linga of about the early 6th century that names eight aspects of Shiva. Inscriptions of 404–487 CE record Gupta kings and local donors including silk weavers from Gujarat.

name: Bhoramdeo Temple
significance: A group of four Shiva temples in Kabirdham district whose 11th-century stone temple is covered in figural and erotic sculpture, earning it the name 'the Khajuraho of Chhattisgarh'. Its brick shrine is far older, and the complex was added to between the 7th and 12th centuries.
story: Local lore says the Gond people of the area worshipped Shiva as Bhoramdeo, and that a Naga chief raised the temple.

name: Rajiv Lochan Temple
significance: A temple of four-armed Vishnu at the confluence town of Rajim, ascribed by inscription to Vilasatunga of the Nala dynasty and dated on palaeographic grounds to the 8th century. It is celebrated for its carved doorways and pillars and for the annual Rajim mela.
story: One legend says king Ratnakar built the temple after Vishnu appeared before him as the lotus-eyed Rajiva-Lochana; another that the mythical king Jagat Pal raised it in a single day.

name: Lakshmana Temple, Sirpur
style: Brick temple on a stone jagati with carved stone sanctum doorway
significance: The earliest dated monument at Sirpur, a brick Vishnu temple of about 600 CE whose stone doorway carries Anantasayana Vishnu, the ten avatars and scenes of daily life, and which set a pattern for later building in the Mahanadi valley.

name: Mahamaya Temple, Ratanpur
significance: A goddess temple at the old Kalachuri capital of Ratanpur, counted among the fifty-two Shakti Peethas and revered as Kosaleswari, presiding deity of ancient Dakshina Kosala and family deity of the Ratanpur rulers.
story: Tradition says the temple stands where king Ratnadeva was granted a vision of the goddess.

name: Rajarani Temple
significance: An 11th-century Kalinga temple in Bhubaneswar with an 18 m clustered spire and some of the finest figure sculpture in Odisha; its empty sanctum means it is kept as a monument rather than a working shrine, and its design influenced later central Indian temples.
story: Local belief derives the name from the Naga and Nagini figures at the entrance, read as a king and queen.

name: Brahmeswara Temple
significance: A Shiva temple with four subsidiary shrines, richly carved inside and out, recorded by inscription as the foundation of the Somavamshi queen Kolavati Devi in the eighteenth regnal year of Udyotakesari.

name: Ananta Vasudeva Temple
significance: The principal Vaishnava temple of old Bhubaneswar, founded in the 13th century by the Eastern Ganga princess Chandrika Devi and unusual in worshipping Krishna, Balarama and Subhadra as complete stone images.

name: Dhauli Shanti Stupa
significance: A white peace pagoda on Dhauli hill above the Daya river, built by the Japan Buddha Sangha and the Kalinga Nippon Buddha Sangha beside Ashoka's rock edicts, at a site long central to Odisha's Buddhist heritage.
story: The hill is widely believed to be where the Kalinga War was fought, the carnage that turned Ashoka to Buddhism.

name: Ratnagiri Mahavihara
builtDisplay: 5th–13th c.; main phase under the Bhauma-Karas
style: Post-Gupta brick with chlorite and khondalite carving
significance: A ruined mahavihara on a hill between the Brahmani and Birupa rivers, the major Buddhist monastery of Odisha and a centre of Tantric and Vajrayana practice, with three main monuments, over seven hundred votive stupas and colossal Buddha heads recovered by excavation.
story: Villagers long took the mounds for the palace of a mythical king and called the site the queen's mound.

name: Udayagiri Buddhist Complex
style: Brick and stone stupas, viharas and chaitya-grihas
significance: The largest Buddhist complex in Odisha, known from inscriptions as Madhavapura Mahavihara, forming with Lalitgiri and Ratnagiri the 'Diamond Triangle' of Odishan Buddhism.

name: Lalitgiri
style: Apsidal brick chaitya-griha; Gandhara and Mathura influence
significance: The oldest Buddhist site in Odisha and part of the Diamond Triangle, with an apsidal chaitya-griha, four monasteries and a stupa that yielded relic caskets, showing occupation from the 3rd century BCE through the Tantric period.
story: The site was once identified with the Pushpagiri Vihara described by Xuanzang, though excavation later placed Pushpagiri at Langudi hill.

name: Biraja Temple
significance: The principal temple of Jajpur and a Shakti Peetha, housing a two-armed Durga slaying Mahishasura; it gives the town its names Viraja Kshetra and Viraja Pitha.
story: The Tantra Chudamani says Sati's navel fell here in the Utkala country.

name: Tara Tarini Temple
significance: A hilltop shrine of the twin goddesses Tara and Tarini on the Kumari hills above the Rushikulya river, counted among the four principal Adi Shakti Pithas of India.
story: It is said to mark the place where Sati's breasts fell.

name: Samaleswari Temple
style: Sandhara order, with a pillared circumambulatory gallery
significance: The presiding goddess temple of Sambalpur on the bank of the Mahanadi, whose square sanctum is ringed by a covered pillared passage; it is the leading pilgrimage centre of western Odisha and the neighbouring parts of Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand.

name: Sakshi Gopal Temple
significance: A medieval Krishna temple between Puri and Bhubaneswar, counted among the sixteen Krishna shrines traditionally ascribed to king Vajranabha; it is known for the Anla Navami festival and for offering wheat-based rather than rice prasada.
story: Krishna is said to have walked from Vrindavan to stand witness to a promise made to a poor young man, turning to stone when the youth looked back to check that the god was following.

name: Nrusinghanath Temple
significance: A 45-foot Kalinga-style temple at the foot of the Gandhamardan hills in western Odisha, built by Baijal Singh Dev of Patna State, where Vishnu is worshipped in the rare feline form of Marjara Kesari.
story: The deity is said to have taken cat form to chase the demon-mouse Musika Daitya into a tunnel beneath the hill, and to guard it still.

name: Mundeshwari Temple
builtDisplay: 6th–7th c.; ASI dates it to 108 CE
significance: A hilltop temple on the Kaimur plateau claimed by the Archaeological Survey of India as one of the oldest continuously worshipped Hindu temples in the country, and the earliest surviving Nagara-style shrine in Bihar, unusual for its octagonal plan.
story: Xuanzang is said to have described a hilltop shrine flashing with light in this area during his travels of 636–638 CE.

name: Jal Mandir, Pawapuri
style: Marble water temple in a lotus tank
significance: A white marble Jain temple standing in the middle of a lotus tank at Pawapuri, built on the spot traditionally identified as the cremation place of Mahavira, who attained nirvana here.
story: The fish of the tank are said to wear gold nose rings, and catching or harming them is forbidden.

name: Vishwa Shanti Stupa, Rajgir
significance: A 120-foot white peace pagoda on Ratnagiri hill at Rajgir, founded by Nichidatsu Fujii and completed in 1969, carrying four gilded Buddha statues for four events of the Buddha's life; it is one of some eighty peace pagodas built worldwide by Nipponzan Myohoji.

name: Relic Stupa and Ashokan Pillar, Vaishali
style: Brick stupa; polished sandstone pillar with lion capital
significance: At Vaishali the Licchavis enshrined one of the eight shares of the Buddha's relics in a brick stupa, among the earliest archaeologically known; nearby at Kolhua stands one of the best-preserved Ashokan pillars, 11 m tall and topped by a single lion.
story: Tradition says the Buddha gave the Licchavis his alms bowl here and conjured the illusion of a river in spate to turn them back.

name: Kesaria Stupa
builtDisplay: present structure Pala, 8th–12th c.; origin c. 250 BCE
significance: One of the tallest and largest Buddhist stupas in India, a terraced mandala-form mound about 32 m high whose visible fabric is of the Pala period over a core attributed to Ashoka; its plan invites comparison with Borobudur.
story: Local tradition connects the stupa with the alms bowl the Buddha gave the Licchavis of Vaishali.

name: Shikharji
builtDisplay: present temples 1768 (Jagat Seth); shrines from the 14th c.
style: Hilltop tonks with marble footprint shrines
significance: The most important Jain tirtha, a 1,365 m hill in Giridih district where twenty of the twenty-four tirthankaras are believed to have attained moksha; its summit shrines are held equally sacred by Digambara and Svetambara Jains.
story: Parshvanatha is said to have attained liberation at the Suvarnabhadra kuta, whose footprint shrine is marked by a chatra.

name: Chhinnamasta Temple, Rajrappa
significance: A tantric shrine of the headless goddess Chhinnamasta at Rajrappa in Ramgarh district, drawing two to three thousand pilgrims a day and known for its distinctive tantric design and animal sacrifice.
story: The goddess is shown standing on the bodies of Kamadeva and Rati on a bed of lotus.

name: Maluti Temples
deity: Moulakshi (Mauliksha), with Shiva, Durga, Kali and Vishnu shrines
significance: A village holding 72 surviving terracotta temples of an original 108, built by the Baj Basanta rajas between the 17th and 19th centuries; the Global Heritage Fund has listed them among the world's most endangered cultural heritage sites.
story: The family goddess Mauliksha is said to be the elder sister of the goddess Tara of Tarapith.

name: Tarapith Temple
significance: A tantric temple of the goddess Tara in Birbhum district with an adjoining cremation ground, revered as a mahapitha and among the busiest pilgrimage sites in West Bengal.
story: The temple is inseparable from the tantric saint Bamakhepa, who worshipped here and lived in the cremation ground beside the Dwarka river.

name: Taraknath Temple, Tarakeswar
significance: An 18th-century atchala Shiva temple in Hooghly district housing a swayambhu linga, one of the busiest Shaiva pilgrimage sites in West Bengal, especially at Shivaratri and the Gajan festival.
story: Local legend says Raja Bharamalla Rao built the temple after a linga was discovered in the nearby jungle.

name: Temple of the Vedic Planetarium, Mayapur
deity: Radha Madhava, with the Pancha Tattva and Narasimha
style: Modern temple with a large dome and Vedic cosmological interior
significance: ISKCON's flagship temple at Mayapur, under construction since 2009 and chaired by Alfred Ford, built around a planetarium presenting Vedic cosmology and intended to serve as the movement's global headquarters.
story: Bhaktivinoda Thakur identified this spot in 1894 as the true birthplace of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu.

name: Hangseshwari Temple
style: Ratna temple with thirteen lotus-bud spires
significance: A five-storeyed ratna temple at Bansberia whose thirteen spires and internal plan were conceived around tantric ideas of the channels of the subtle body. Begun by Raja Nrisinhadeb Roy in 1799, it was completed by his widow Rani Sankari in 1814.
