significance: One of Bhutan's oldest temples, dedicated to Maitreya and ascribed to the Tibetan king Songtsen Gampo in 659 CE, in the same group as the Jokhang at Lhasa and Kyichu in Paro. Padmasambhava is said to have visited it and King Sindhu Raja to have restored it; repaired and rebuilt many times since, it remains an active pilgrimage temple and hosts the Jambay Lhakhang Drup festival each October.
story: The legend says Songtsen Gampo raised 108 temples in a single day across Tibet, Bhutan and the borderlands to pin down a supine ogress whose limbs were blocking the spread of Buddhism, this temple standing on one of those points.

name: Kurjey Lhakhang
significance: A three-temple monastery complex in Bhutan's Bumthang valley, the oldest of whose shrines was raised by king Sindhu Raja beside a meditation cave. It also serves as the resting place of the remains of Bhutan's first three kings.
story: Oral tradition holds that Padmasambhava subdued the local deity Shelging Karpo here and left the imprint of his body in the cave, from which the site takes its name.

name: Gangteng Monastery
significance: Founded in 1613 by Gyalse Pema Thinley, grandson of the treasure-revealer Pema Lingpa, this fortress-like monastery above the Phobjikha valley is the principal seat of the Pema Lingpa tradition and one of Bhutan's two main Nyingma centres. It was extensively restored between 2002 and 2008 with the support of the fourth king, Jigme Singye Wangchuck.
story: Local accounts tell that a guardian deity caused a landslide that exposed the stone needed to build the monastery, and that the valley's black-necked cranes circle it three times on arrival and again before returning to Tibet.

name: Buddha Dordenma
significance: A 54-metre bronze Shakyamuni Buddha seated on a hill above Thimphu, cast by the Aerosun Corporation of Nanjing and completed on 25 September 2015 to mark the sixtieth anniversary of King Jigme Singye Wangchuck. Its base houses some 100,000 smaller bronze Buddha images.
story: The statue is held to fulfil a prophecy attributed to the 20th-century yogi Sonam Zangpo, and an older terma of Guru Rinpoche, that a great image would be raised in Bhutan to bestow blessings, peace and happiness.

name: Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi
deity: Sacred Bodhi tree of the Buddha
significance: A sacred fig grown from a cutting of the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya, planted in the royal park at Anuradhapura in 288 BCE by King Devanampiya Tissa and protected by later rulers including Vasabha, Sena II and Kirti Sri Rajasinha. Raised on a terrace some 6.5 metres above ground and ringed by walls and companion trees, it draws millions of pilgrims a year.
story: Sri Lankan tradition holds that the southern branch of the original Bodhi tree was carried to the island by the Buddhist nun Sanghamitta, daughter of the emperor Ashoka.

name: Dambulla Cave Temple
significance: Five rock-cut caves on a granite outcrop that King Valagamba converted into a monastery in the first century BCE, gilded and filled with some seventy Buddha images by Nissanka Malla in 1190, and painted under the Kandyan king Kirti Sri Rajasinha in the 18th century. Inscribed by UNESCO in 1991, it is the best-preserved ancient monastic complex in Sri Lanka and remains in use.
story: Local tradition credits Vishnu with creating the caves by divine power, and holds that the water dripping in the second cave has healing power.

name: Mihintale
deity: Gautama Buddha; associated with Arahant Mahinda
builtDisplay: 3rd c. BCE onwards; additions to 10th c.
significance: A hill of stupas, drip-ledged caves and monastic ruins near Anuradhapura where, by chronicle tradition, the monk Mahinda met King Devanampiyatissa on the Poson full-moon day and preached the Buddha's doctrine, marking the arrival of Buddhism in Sri Lanka. Its inscriptions and structures span the 3rd century BCE to the 10th century CE, with works recorded under rulers from Suratissa to Mihindu.
story: The Mahavamsa relates that Mahinda travelled through the air and alighted on the rock of Aradhana Gala, where he first met the king.

name: Kelaniya Raja Maha Vihara
significance: A Buddhist temple on the Kelani river near Colombo, traditionally traced to the Naga king Maniakkika and closely bound up with the fortunes of successive Sri Lankan states. It was patronised by the Kandyan king Kirti Sri Rajasingha and refurbished in the early 20th century with support from Helena Wijewardene.
story: Buddhist tradition holds that the Buddha visited Kelaniya in the eighth year after his enlightenment to settle a dispute, and that the Naga kings afterwards enshrined the gem-studded throne he had used.

name: Gal Vihara
significance: A face of granite gneiss at Polonnaruwa carved with four large Buddha images, seated, standing and reclining, commissioned by King Parakramabahu I in the 12th century. He convened a monastic council here to reconcile the island's three fraternities and had the resulting code of conduct cut into the rock; the figures are regarded as high points of Sinhalese sculpture.

name: Jetavanaramaya
builtDisplay: begun 3rd c. under Mahasena, completed by Kithsirimevan
significance: A colossal brick stupa at Anuradhapura begun by King Mahasena in the late 3rd century and finished by his son Kithsirimevan, raised amid the rivalry between the Mahavihara and Mahayana factions. At about 122 metres it was once the tallest stupa in the world and among the tallest structures of antiquity; Parakramabahu I renovated it in the 12th century.
story: A piece of a sash worn by the Buddha is believed to be the relic enshrined within it, and the surrounding forest is said to be named Jetavana after the grove where Mahinda preached.

name: Abhayagiri Vihara
deity: Gautama Buddha; once housed the Tooth Relic
significance: One of the great monastic cities of ancient Anuradhapura, whose dagaba was raised by King Valagamba during his second reign in the late 1st century BCE and which grew into a centre where Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana learning coexisted. Its monks maintained scholarly links with China, Java and Kashmir, and from the 4th century the Buddha's Tooth Relic was shown here.
story: Tradition relates that Valagamba, taunted by a Jain ascetic named Giri as he fled a battle, vowed to build a monastery on the spot and fulfilled the oath fourteen years later on regaining his throne.

name: Munneswaram Temple
builtDisplay: attested by c. 1000 CE; present form 1753
significance: A Shiva temple complex near Chilaw attested at least since about 1000 CE and patronised in turn by the kings of Kotte, Sitawaka and Kandy, reaching its present form under Kirti Sri Rajasinghe in 1753. One of the island's Pancha Ishwaram shrines, it comprises five structures including a Buddhist temple, with subsidiary shrines to Ganesha, Aiyanar and Kali.
story: Tamil tradition links the temple to Rama of the Ramayana, while Sinhala Buddhist myth tells of the goddess Kali coming ashore at Chilaw and settling at Munneswaram, where the deity Pattini restrained her from harming people.

name: Naguleswaram Temple
significance: The northernmost of Sri Lanka's Pancha Ishwaram Shiva temples, standing beside the Keerimalai springs north of Jaffna and counted among the oldest shrines of the region. Destroyed by the Portuguese in 1621 and restored by Arumuka Navalar in 1894, it was bombed during the civil war and reconstructed by February 2012.
story: The sage Nagula Muni, whose body had shrivelled from austerities, is said to have been cured by bathing in the springs and to have founded the shrine to the lingam in gratitude.

name: Seetha Amman Temple
significance: A Vaishnavite temple to Sita at Seetha Eliya near Nuwara Eliya, grown from a simple site where unshaped stones stood for the deities into a full temple built by South Indian Tamil plantation workers, who still maintain it. It is a principal stop on Sri Lanka's Ramayana pilgrimage circuit and has been promoted by Ramayana advocacy groups in India.
story: The Ramayana places Sita's captivity under Ravana at this spot and holds that Hanuman found her here and gave her Rama's ring as a token of hope.

name: Shri Varun Dev Mandir
significance: A temple on Manora Island off Karachi, said to be the only shrine dedicated to Varuna in Pakistan and of particular importance to Sindhi Hindus. Its present structure was renovated around 1917-18 and the building was restored again in 2018 by the Sindh Exploration and Adventure Society.
story: Tradition holds that the temple was commissioned around the 16th century after the wealthy sailor Bhojomal Nenshi Bhatia bought Manora Island from the Khan of Kalat.

name: Panchmukhi Hanuman Temple
significance: A Hindu temple in Soldier Bazaar, Karachi, holding a 2.5-metre five-faced Hanuman image and protected as a national heritage site under the Sindh Cultural Heritage (Preservation) Act of 1994. Renovation begun in 2012 and further work in 2019 uncovered more centuries-old statuary at the site.
story: Devotees hold that Rama visited this spot during his exile and that the Hanuman image here was divinely revealed rather than made by human hands.

name: Goraknath Temple
significance: A Hindu temple at the centre of the Gor Khatri compound in Peshawar, dedicated to Guru Gorakhnath, founder of the Kanphata Jogi order, and dated to 1851. Closed for decades, it was reopened in 2011 on the order of the Peshawar High Court and declared a heritage site; it is one of very few Hindu temples still standing in the city.

name: Mankiala Stupa
significance: A large Buddhist stupa on the Potohar plateau south-east of Rawalpindi, associated by inscription with the Kushan emperor Kanishka, who is recorded as having visited it often. It was described by Mountstuart Elphinstone in his memoir of 1815 and opened in 1830 by Jean-Baptiste Ventura, whose relic finds were removed to the British Museum under British rule.
story: Jataka tradition holds that the stupa marks the spot where Prince Sattva, an earlier birth of the Buddha, gave parts of his own body to feed seven starving tiger cubs.

name: Sadh Belo
deity: Shiva, with shrines to Annapurna, Hanuman and Ganesha
significance: A temple complex on an island in the Indus at Sukkur, settled in 1823 by the Udasi ascetic Baba Bankhandi Maharaj and built up from 1899 under the eighth gaddi nashin Sant Harnam Das. Its Teerath Asthan is described as the largest Hindu temple in Pakistan, and the annual Bankhandi Maharaj mela draws thousands of pilgrims for three days of free lodging and food.
story: Bankhandi is said to have been visited in a dream by the goddess Annapurna, who gave him a kamandal with the promise that while it stayed on the island the community kitchen would never lack grain.

name: Mes Aynak
significance: An extensive ancient Buddhist settlement in Logar province with monasteries, dwellings and more than 400 Buddha statues spread over some 40 hectares, at its height between the 5th and 7th centuries CE. Coins of the Alchon rulers Khingila and Mehama date part of the occupation to around 450-500 CE; the site declined from the 8th century and has since been excavated under the threat of copper mining.

name: Takht-e Rostam
significance: A Buddhist stupa and monastery near Samangan hewn entirely out of the bedrock in the 3rd-4th centuries CE under the Kushano-Sasanians. After the Muslim conquests the abandoned complex was absorbed into Persian legend, which supplied its present name.
story: Persian tradition holds that the hero Rostam of Ferdowsi's Shahnameh travelled to the kingdom of Samangan and stayed with its king at this place.

name: Adinath Temple, Maheshkhali
significance: A Shiva temple on the summit of Mainak hill on Maheshkhali island off Cox's Bazar. It is best known for the thirteen-day fair held at the foot of the hill in the month of Phalgun, which draws thousands of pilgrims from across Bangladesh.

name: Puthia Temple Complex
deity: Krishna, Shiva and Jagannath across several temples
significance: The largest cluster of historic Hindu temples in Bangladesh, raised at Puthia in Rajshahi by the zamindars and rajas of the Puthia Raj family, whose estate was established in the 16th century. It includes the Pancha Ratna Govinda temple, the Bhubaneshwar Shiva temple built by Rani Bhubonmoyee Devi in 1823, and several smaller shrines faced with terracotta ornament.

name: Ramna Kali Mandir
significance: A Kali temple in the Ramna area of Dhaka, first raised in the Mughal period and much enlarged in the early 20th century under Rani Bilashmoni Debi, when it stood among the city's tallest landmarks. The complex was destroyed by the Pakistan Army on 27 March 1971 during the Liberation War; the rebuilt temple was inaugurated on 17 December 2021.
story: Nepalese folklore holds that the devotees who founded the temple had come to Bengal from the Himalayas.

name: Shalban Vihara
significance: A square Buddhist monastery of 115 monastic cells around a central shrine on the Mainamati-Lalmai ridge near Comilla, attributed to Bhava Deva, the fourth ruler of the early Deva dynasty. It remained in use into the 12th century and excavation has yielded artefacts spanning the 7th to 12th centuries.

name: Mahasthangarh
deity: Ancient city and Buddhist monastic site (Vasu Vihara)
significance: A fortified ancient city near Bogra identified with Pundranagara, capital of the Pundra kingdom, occupied from not later than the 3rd century BCE until its fortified area fell out of use in the 8th century CE. Excavations in and around the citadel, including the Buddhist monastery of Vasu Vihara, have exposed remains of the Mauryan, Gupta and later periods.
story: Local tradition tells of the saint Shah Sultan Balkhi Mahisawar, who arrived riding a fish and defeated King Parasuram after having the Jiat Kunda pool, whose water revived the king's fallen soldiers, contaminated so that it lost its power.

name: Sulamani Temple
significance: A brick-and-stone temple at Bagan built in 1183 by King Narapatisithu, close in design to the Thatbyinnyu, influenced by the Dhammayangyi and in turn a model for the later Htilominlo. Damaged by the earthquake of 1975 and rebuilt in 1994, it retains interior frescoes and is one of Bagan's most visited monuments.

name: Dhammayangyi Temple
significance: The largest and widest temple at Bagan, begun by King Narathu in 1167 and left unfinished when he was assassinated three years later. Its inner corridors were bricked up at some later point for reasons never established, so only the outer passages can be entered.
story: The chronicles say Narathu came to the throne by killing his father and elder brother, and that he raised this vast temple to atone for those crimes.

name: Thatbyinnyu Temple
significance: The tallest temple at Bagan, a five-storeyed brick and stucco structure about 61 metres high crowned by a sikhara tower, completed in 1150-51 in the reign of King Sithu I. It is read by scholars as a high point of Pagan-period architecture, and has been under restoration since the earthquake of 2016.

name: Htilominlo Temple
significance: A three-storeyed red-brick temple 46 metres high at Bagan, completed in 1211 under King Htilominlo, also known as Nandaungmya. Four Buddha images face the cardinal directions on its ground floor, and it is noted for its elaborate plaster mouldings.

name: Sule Pagoda
builtDisplay: enlarged 15th c. under Shin Sawbu; traditionally far older
significance: An octagonal gilded stupa about 44 metres high at the centre of downtown Yangon, whose main structure was enlarged by Queen Shin Sawbu between 1453 and 1472. When Lt. Alexander Fraser laid out the colonial street grid in the mid-19th century he made the pagoda its hub, and it has since served as a rallying point in the 1988 and 2007 uprisings.
story: Legend says the nat Sularata, whose eyelids had to be propped open, showed King Okkalapa where three earlier Buddhas had buried relics, and the pagoda was raised there over a hair of the Buddha given to the merchants Trapusa and Bahalika.

name: Botataung Pagoda
significance: A riverside pagoda in Yangon, destroyed by Allied bombing on 8 November 1943 and rebuilt from 4 January 1948, the day of Myanmar's independence. Clearing the ruins uncovered a relic chamber whose contents, including what is venerated as a hair of the Buddha, are now displayed inside the hollow, walk-through stupa.
story: Its name, meaning a thousand military officers, is said to come from the thousand officers who formed a guard of honour when relics of the Buddha were brought here from India more than two thousand years ago.

name: Kuthodaw Pagoda
significance: A stupa and inscription complex at the foot of Mandalay Hill begun by King Mindon Min in 1860, its 57-metre main stupa modelled on the Shwezigon at Nyaung-U. Its 729 marble slabs, each housed in a small shrine, carry the Tipitaka in stone and are often called the world's largest book; they were opened to the public in 1868 and served the Fifth Buddhist Synod.

name: Shwenandaw Monastery
significance: A teak monastery in Mandalay created in 1878, when King Thibaw Min had his father King Mindon's former royal apartment taken down and re-erected outside the palace as a memorial. It is the only major original structure of the Mandalay royal palace still standing.
story: Thibaw is said to have moved the building because he believed it haunted by his father's spirit; he used it for meditation, and the couch on which he sat is still shown there.

name: Shite-thaung Temple
significance: A fortress-like temple on the western face of Pokhaung hill at Mrauk U, built in 1535-36 by King Min Bin to commemorate his conquest of Bengal. Known as the Temple of 80,000 Buddha Images and also as the Temple of Victory, it has a central bell-shaped stupa with four corner stupas and three concentric maze-like corridors lined with Buddha figures and relief carving.

name: Kaunghmudaw Pagoda
significance: A white stupa 46 metres high near Sagaing, built between April 1636 and May 1648 under King Thalun of the Restored Toungoo kingdom. Its formal name Yaza Mani Sula refers to the relics enshrined in its chamber, and its rounded, egg-shaped dome, modelled on the Ruwanwelisaya in Sri Lanka, sets it apart from the usual Burmese bell profile.
story: Local belief holds that the relic chamber contains the Buddha's lower left tooth, eleven hair relics and an alms bowl, and that the dome was raised around a 7.3-metre marble Buddha image.

name: Wat Phra Si Sanphet
significance: The royal chapel of the Ayutthaya palace, made a sacred precinct by King Borommatrailokkanat in 1448 on the site of the palace founded by Ramathibodi I in 1350, and marked by three bell-shaped chedis raised between 1492 and 1529. Reserved for the royal family and once housing an enormous gold-covered Buddha, it was destroyed in the Burmese sack of 1767.

name: Wat Mahathat, Ayutthaya
significance: A royal relic monastery in the centre of Ayutthaya, recorded in the royal chronicles as founded in 1374 by Borommarachathirat I together with the elder Thammakanlayan and expanded ten years later by his nephew Ramesuan. Now a ruin, it is among the most important temple sites of the UNESCO-listed historic city.

name: Wat Chaiwatthanaram
significance: A riverside temple west of Ayutthaya island completed in 1630 as the first foundation of King Prasat Thong's reign, in memory of his mother's residence there. Built to a Khmer plan with a 35-metre central prang ringed by four lesser prangs and eight chedi-shaped chapels carrying Jataka reliefs, it lay abandoned after the fall of Ayutthaya in 1767 until restoration began in 1987.

name: Wat Traimit
deity: Gautama Buddha (Phra Phuttha Maha Suwanna Patimakon, the Golden Buddha)
significance: A temple in Bangkok's Chinatown, probably founded in the reign of Rama III, largely rebuilt in the 1930s-40s and renamed Wat Traimit Witthayaram in 1940. It enshrines the Phra Phuttha Maha Suwanna Patimakon, a solid-gold Buddha brought here in 1935 whose gold core came to light only when the plaster covering it broke during a move in 1955; the image now sits in a four-storey marble-clad mondop.
story: Oral history holds that the temple was founded by three Chinese friends, which is said to explain its name.

name: Wat Saket
builtDisplay: 19th c.; Golden Mount completed under Rama V
significance: A Bangkok temple of Ayutthaya-period origin, known as Wat Sakae until King Rama I renovated and renamed it, and crowned by the Golden Mount, an artificial hill and chedi begun under Rama III and completed under Rama V. Through the 19th century it was the city's principal cremation ground, overwhelmed by the dead during the cholera epidemics between 1820 and 1881.
story: The vultures of Wat Saket, the flocks that fed on corpses left exposed during those epidemics, passed into Bangkok speech as a byword for death and gave rise to ghost stories about the place.

name: Wat Benchamabophit
significance: Commissioned by King Chulalongkorn in 1899 next to his new Dusit Palace and finished in 1911, this royal monastery was designed by Prince Narisara Nuwattiwong and faced in imported Carrara marble, giving it its popular name, the Marble Temple. Its cruciform ordination hall holds a Sukhothai-style principal Buddha cast from melted brass cannon, beneath which the king's ashes are interred, and a surrounding gallery displays 52 Buddha images in differing postures.

name: Erawan Shrine
significance: A public shrine in central Bangkok housing a four-faced image of Phra Phrom, the Thai form of Brahma, which the Fine Arts Department designed and enshrined on 9 November 1956 for the state-owned Erawan Hotel. It has remained one of the city's busiest devotional sites even after the original hotel was demolished in 1987 and replaced by the Grand Hyatt Erawan, and it is a much-cited example of Hindu, Buddhist and Thai animist worship converging at one altar.
story: The shrine is said to have been raised to offset the bad karma of laying the hotel's foundation on an inauspicious date, after which the accidents and delays that had plagued the building work reportedly stopped.

name: Sri Maha Mariamman Temple, Bangkok
significance: Founded in 1879 by the Tamil migrant Vaithi Padayatchi, this Silom temple is the oldest and most important Hindu shrine in Thailand, serving the Tamil community that settled in Bangkok as gem traders and cattle keepers from the late 1850s onward. A six-metre gopura carved with deity figures fronts the complex, and a gilded copper dome covers the main sanctum, with subsidiary shrines to Ganesha, Murugan, Shiva, Vishnu, Lakshmi, Kali, Saraswati and Nataraja.

name: Wat Rong Khun (White Temple)
significance: The original temple here had fallen into disrepair by the end of the twentieth century, and the Chiang Rai national artist Chalermchai Kositpipat rebuilt it entirely at his own expense as an offering to the Buddha, opening it to visitors in 1997 and funding it with more than 40 million baht of his own money. Its all-white, mirror-inlaid buildings are laid out as a walk-through allegory, with a bridge over a pit of reaching hands standing for the passage beyond desire; work is projected to continue until about 2070, and an engineering survey confirmed the structure sound after a 2014 earthquake.

name: Wat Phra That Lampang Luang
significance: A walled hilltop monastery founded in the fifteenth century and reckoned among the most authentic surviving examples of Lanna architecture in northern Thailand, enshrining relics said to include a hair of the Buddha and ashes from his forehead and neck. In 1732 Phraya Chaisongkhram launched his surprise attack on the Burmese garrison occupying Lampang from inside the compound, killing their commander and founding the Chet Ton dynasty; bullet damage from the fight is still shown to visitors.
story: Local tradition holds that the Buddha passed this way, accepted honey offered in a bamboo tube by Lawa people, foretold that the place would become the city of Lampakappa Nakhon, and left a hair relic that devotees believe lies beneath the central chedi.

name: Wat Phra That Hariphunchai
significance: The chief Theravada monastery of Lamphun, whose stupa is traced to about 897 in the Hariphunchai kingdom and whose present compound was founded by King Athitayarat in 1044. King Tilokaraja of Lanna rebuilt much of it in 1443 and the monk Khru Ba Sriwichai led further restoration in the 1930s; the 46-metre Chedi Suwanna, a fifteenth-century Buddha image, a nineteenth-century library and a bronze gong of 1860 stand within the walls.
story: A stone in the south-western corner of the compound bears four footprint impressions that worshippers take as proof of a visit by the Buddha.

name: Prasat Muang Tam
significance: A tenth-century Khmer sanctuary in Prakhon Chai district dedicated principally to Shiva, with Vishnu also worshipped there. Unusually for a Khmer temple it is flat rather than pyramidal, its concentric enclosures separated by L-shaped ponds; kala carvings on the lintels supply much of the dating evidence, some outer gopura lintels were left unfinished, and all the towers except the central one have been restored.

name: Sdok Kok Thom
significance: A red sandstone and laterite temple in Sa Kaeo province built under Udayadityavarman II, important less for its scale than for its stele, inscription K.235 of 1053, which records nine generations of a priestly family serving Khmer kings as royal chaplains and is a primary source for Angkorian dynastic history. The stele was taken to the national museum in Bangkok in the 1920s and damaged by fire in 1960; the site itself served as a refugee camp after 1978 before restoration began in the 1990s.
story: The inscription describes a brahmin named Hiranyadaman being summoned by the king to perform a rite that would make it impossible for the land of the Kambuja to owe allegiance to Java.

name: Wat Xieng Thong
significance: Built by King Setthathirath of Lan Xang on the tip of the Luang Prabang peninsula between the Mekong and the Nam Khan, this monastery served as a royal sanctuary until 1975, hosting coronations, festivals, relic veneration and a manuscript library. It escaped the sacking of the city in 1887 because the Black Flag commander had trained there as a monk and used it as his headquarters; the Tripitaka library was added in 1880 and the drum tower in 1961.

name: Wat Si Saket
significance: Ordered by King Anouvong in 1818, this monastery is probably the oldest structure still standing in Vientiane, its cloister walls lined with more than two thousand ceramic and silver Buddha images beneath an ornate five-tiered roof. It may have survived the destruction that followed Anouvong's revolt of 1827 precisely because Siamese forces took it over as their headquarters; the French administration restored it in 1924 and 1930, and part of it now serves as a museum.

name: Preah Khan
significance: Founded by Jayavarman VII on the ground where he defeated the invading Cham in 1181 and completed in 1191, Preah Khan was named Nagara Jayasri, the holy city of victory, and its central image of Avalokiteshvara portrayed the king's father. Flat in plan, with concentric rectangular galleries around the Buddhist sanctuary and Hindu satellite shrines, it functioned as a city, monastery and university said to have supported nearly a hundred thousand attendants before royal patronage lapsed after the fifteenth century; it was cleared in 1927–1932 and has been conserved by the World Monuments Fund since 1991.

name: Neak Pean
significance: An artificial island shrine set in the Jayatataka baray beside Preah Khan, built under Jayavarman VII and counted among the hospitals of his reign: bathers were understood to have the elements within them rebalanced and their disease cured. Four linked pools stand for water, earth, fire and wind, each with its own spout in the form of an elephant, bull, horse or lion, and the Chinese envoy Zhou Daguan recorded the site during his visit to Angkor in the late thirteenth century.
story: The pools are held to represent Anavatapta, a mythical Himalayan lake whose waters cure every illness, and the surviving horse figure is Balaha, the form Avalokiteshvara took to carry shipwrecked sailors away from the ogresses of Tamradvipa.

name: Pre Rup
significance: The state temple of King Rajendravarman, dedicated in 961 or early 962 and built as a temple-mountain of brick, laterite and sandstone south of the East Baray on an axis with the East Mebon. Two enclosure walls surround an outer platform of about 117 by 127 metres, from which a three-tiered pyramid rises to a summit carrying five towers in quincunx, the central one holding the main sanctuary and the corner towers once housing images of Lakshmi, Uma and Vishnu.
story: Its modern name means to turn the body, from a widespread Cambodian belief that funerals were held here and the ashes ritually rotated to face each direction in turn as the rite proceeded.

name: East Mebon
significance: Dedicated in 953 by King Rajendravarman to Shiva and to the memory of his parents, this temple stands on what was an island at the centre of the East Baray, now a dry reservoir. Built of sandstone, brick, laterite and stucco with two enclosing walls and three tiers, it carries a central tower flanked by four corner towers, free-standing stone elephants at the terrace corners, and four landing stages at its base showing that it was once reached by boat.

name: Phnom Bakheng
significance: Raised between 889 and 910 by Yasovarman I as the state temple of Yasodharapura, the capital he founded after moving the court from Hariharalaya, this hilltop temple-mountain predates Angkor Wat by two centuries. A moat ringed the hill and avenues ran out from it in the cardinal directions; its seven levels were read as the seven heavens, its 108 towers as lunar cycles and the 33 towers visible from the centre as the gods of Mount Meru, which the whole structure represents. Monumental Buddha sculpture was added when the site later passed to Buddhist use, and the World Monuments Fund has worked on its conservation since 2004.

name: Ta Som
deity: Dharanindravarman II, deified father of Jayavarman VII
significance: A small Bayon-style temple north-east of Angkor Thom, built at the close of the twelfth century by Jayavarman VII and dedicated to his father Dharanindravarman II, who ruled from 1150 to 1160. Its gopuras carry the four-faced towers characteristic of the style; the site was left largely unrestored until the World Monuments Fund began stabilisation in 1998, and by 2007 clearance and documentation had opened access from all four sides and allowed damaged sandstone to be reset. A strangler fig grown down through the blocks of the eastern outer gopura is its best-known feature.

name: Banteay Kdei
significance: A Buddhist monastic complex laid out under Jayavarman VII over the remains of a tenth-century temple, similar in plan to Ta Prohm and Preah Khan but smaller and simpler. Monks lived here until the 1960s; poor-quality sandstone and faulty construction left it badly decayed, Henri Marchal began conservation in 1920, and excavations by Sophia University between 1992 and 2002 recovered 274 fragments of buried Buddhist sandstone statuary.

name: Bakong
significance: Completed in 881 under Indravarman I as the state temple of Hariharalaya, the capital now called Roluos, Bakong is the earliest sandstone temple-mountain the Khmer built and the model for the pyramids that followed at Angkor. Its five-tiered central pyramid measures roughly 65 by 67 metres at the base and once held a linga at the summit; the present central tower is a twelfth-century replacement reflecting later religious change, and the pyramid was restored in the 1930s by the French conservator Maurice Glaize.
story: The plan is read as a model of the cosmos, its moats standing for the mythical oceans and its enclosing walls and terraces for the mountain ranges that ring Mount Meru.

name: Preah Ko
significance: Built in 879 by Indravarman I soon after his accession, Preah Ko sets six brick towers in two rows on a single sandstone platform, its sanctuaries honouring three deified male ancestors and their wives in association with Shiva; the front central tower commemorates Jayavarman II, who founded the Khmer empire in 802. The towers were restored in the early 1990s with German government funding.

name: Beng Mealea
significance: A large sandstone temple some 40 kilometres east of the main Angkor group whose written history is lost; it is placed in the reign of Suryavarman II purely on the strength of an architectural style identical to Angkor Wat. Three enclosing galleries with cruciform cloisters and seven-headed naga balustrades surround the central sanctuary, and the temple stood at the heart of a town ringed by a moat about 1,025 by 875 metres and 45 metres wide. It remains largely unrestored and heavily overgrown, though its carvings include the Churning of the Ocean of Milk and other Vaishnava scenes alongside some Buddhist motifs.

name: Banteay Chhmar
significance: One of the largest and most remote foundations of Jayavarman VII's great building programme, flourishing in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries in what is now Banteay Meanchey province. Its carvings include multi-armed dancing Heruka figures and other tantric imagery alongside Lokeshvara, and the settlement around it, with its moats and water channels, notably lacks the formal grid that ordered most Angkorian centres. The site is on UNESCO's tentative list and has suffered heavy looting in recent decades.

name: Prasat Thom, Koh Ker
significance: The principal temple of Koh Ker, the capital Jayavarman IV held while the Khmer court was away from Angkor, with inscriptions recording the consecration in 921 of a Shiva-linga worshipped as Tribhuvaneshvara, lord of the threefold world. Parts including the moat and inner enclosure appear to predate 921 and were absorbed into the expansion under Jayavarman IV. Two walls, brick within and laterite without at 66 by 55 metres, enclose a court holding the sanctuary, two libraries, nine linga towers in two rows and twelve smaller prasats grouped in threes, all in the sharply distinct Koh Ker style.

name: Phnom Chisor
significance: An eleventh-century Angkorian foundation of Suryavarman I crowning a 133-metre hill in Takeo province, dedicated to Shiva and in part to Vishnu, and reached by a stair of roughly 610 steps. Six brick shrines make up the complex, the central one about 60 by 50 metres within two galleries, with sandstone construction extending some 400 metres across the summit. It was repaired in 1917 under French Indochina, wrecked during the fighting of the 1970s and rebuilt in 1979, and is now visited by Buddhist and Hindu pilgrims alike.

name: Wat Phnom
significance: The Theravada temple on the artificial hill from which Phnom Penh takes its name, traditionally founded in 1372 by the woman known as Lady Penh and rebuilt repeatedly through the nineteenth century and again in 1926. King Ponhea Yat moved the Cambodian capital here in 1397 and a large stupa was later raised for him at the summit; the hill and sanctuary together stand 46 metres high, and the shrine holds four Buddha images and one of Vishnu.
story: Lady Penh is said to have gone down to the river in the rain to bathe and found a floating koki tree carrying five statues, which she housed in a shrine built on a mound raised for the purpose.

name: Po Klong Garai
deity: Shiva (mukhalinga venerated as King Po Klaung Garai)
significance: A hilltop Cham brick group above Phan Rang raised toward the end of the thirteenth century under Jaya Simhavarman III, though earlier steles, including one of 1050 commemorating a Cham victory over Panduranga, suggest it replaced or enlarged older structures. Three brick towers survive, a three-storeyed main tower, a smaller gate tower and a long saddle-roofed building, and the sanctum holds a sixteenth- or seventeenth-century mukhalinga that Cham worshippers treat as an image of the king himself. The site remains in active use for Cham festivals.
story: Po Klong Garai, whose name means great water-dragon sovereign, is remembered as a cowherd who rose to the throne, ruled wisely, turned back a Khmer invasion by winning a tower-building contest, and became a protective deity after his death.

name: Thien Mu Pagoda
deity: Maitreya Buddha, with Manjushri and Samantabhadra
significance: Founded in 1601 on the order of Nguyen Hoang, governor of Thuan Hoa, on a hill above the Perfume River, and enlarged by successive Nguyen rulers in 1665, 1695–96 and 1714. Its cult absorbed an earlier Cham goddess, Po Nagar, under the name Thien Mu, the Celestial Lady; the seven-storeyed octagonal brick tower Phuoc Duyen rises 21 metres over the site. A cyclone wrecked much of it in 1904 and rebuilding began in 1907, and in 1963 it became a centre of Buddhist protest against the Diem government.
story: An old woman in red and blue is said to have appeared on the hill, foretold that a lord would come and raise a pagoda there, and then vanished.

name: One Pillar Pagoda
significance: Built in 1049 by Emperor Ly Thai Tong and refined in 1105 under Ly Nhan Tong, this small hexagonal shrine to Avalokiteshvara stands on a single stone pillar 1.25 metres across and 4 metres high, shaped so that the whole rises like a lotus, the Buddhist emblem of purity. Destroyed in 1954, it was rebuilt the following year by North Vietnam's Ministry of Culture; a replica was raised near Saigon in the late 1950s.
story: The emperor is said to have dreamed of Avalokiteshvara seated on a lotus handing him a son; a son was born after he married a peasant girl, and he built the lotus-shaped shrine in thanks.

name: Perfume Pagoda
significance: A scattered complex of shrines and cave sanctuaries in the limestone Huong Tich hills south-west of Hanoi, with a temple recorded here in the reign of Le Thanh Tong in the fifteenth century and a stele documenting the terraces and shrines built in 1686 under Le Hy Tong. Bronze images were cast in 1767 and replaced in 1793; buildings damaged in the French and American wars were repaired, the bell tower in 1986 and the gateway in 1994. It draws one of the largest pilgrim festivals in northern Vietnam.
story: The bodhisattva Quan Am is said to have travelled south and settled at Huong Tich in order to save human souls, and a stone at nearby Phat Tich is held to preserve her footprint.

name: Bai Dinh Temple
significance: A vast Buddhist complex in Gia Vien district combining an older mountainside temple with a new 700-hectare precinct built between 2003 and 2010, among the largest in Vietnam. Its halls follow traditional Vietnamese forms, with corner eaves curving up like a phoenix tail, the Tam The hall rising 34 metres; stone, timber and tiles were sourced locally and the fittings made by regional craft villages. Mountain spirits are venerated at the site alongside the Buddhas.

name: Mariamman Temple, Ho Chi Minh City
significance: Built in the late nineteenth century by Nagarathar merchants from Tamil Nadu, with Palaniappa Chettiar named as its founder, this is the principal Hindu temple of Ho Chi Minh City. A raja-gopuram about 12 metres high fronts a mandapam, and deity figures line the outer walls. It now serves some fifty Tamil families, but most of those who come to worship are Vietnamese or Sino-Vietnamese devotees of Mariamman.

name: Candi Sewu
builtDisplay: c. 792 (Rakai Panangkaran, completed under King Indra)
significance: The second-largest Buddhist temple compound in Indonesia, named Manjusrigrha, the house of Manjushri, in an inscription of about 792; work began under Rakai Panangkaran and was completed under King Indra. Its 249 shrines are set out as a mandala representing the universe, and it was the kingdom's chief Buddhist sanctuary before Borobudur and Prambanan rose nearby. Volcanic debris buried the site, which was rediscovered early in the nineteenth century, looted during the Java War, photographed by 1867 and systematically reconstructed from 1908.
story: Local folklore held that the temples were raised in a single night by a host of demons commanded by Bandung Bondowoso, part of the Loro Jonggrang legend attached to nearby Prambanan.

name: Candi Plaosan
significance: A Buddhist compound of the mid-ninth century, dated by inscriptions to between 825 and 850 and attributed to Sri Kahulunnan, or Pramodhawardhani, daughter of Samaratungga of the Sailendra line. It comprises 174 structures, 116 stupas and 58 shrines, in two groups, Plaosan Lor to the north and Plaosan Kidul to the south, originally a single complex now divided by a road. The 2006 Java earthquake caused damage, and the excavations that followed recovered significant finds.

name: Candi Kalasan
significance: Dated by its own inscription to 778, Kalasan was raised as the Tarabhavanam, a holy building for the goddess Tara, together with a monastery, after a Sailendra preceptor persuaded Maharaja Panangkaran to found it. The shrine is cross-shaped, a twelve-cornered polygon with octagonal roof stages, and is among the oldest Buddhist candi on the Prambanan plain; despite Dutch-era repairs it is now in poor condition and less well kept than its famous neighbours.

name: Candi Mendut
significance: The oldest of the three aligned temples that include Pawon and Borobudur, built early in the ninth century under King Indra of the Sailendra dynasty; the Karangtengah inscription of 824 mentions the founding of a sacred building called the bamboo forest, generally identified with it. Its chamber holds three large stone images, the Dhyani Buddha Vairocana flanked by Avalokiteshvara and Vajrapani. Found in ruins in 1836, it was restored between 1897 and 1925 and inscribed with the Borobudur Temple Compounds as a World Heritage Site in 1991; women still pray before its relief of Hariti, protector of children, when hoping for a child.

name: Candi Pawon
significance: A small ninth-century Sailendra shrine standing on the straight line that joins Borobudur and Mendut, credited to the architect Gunadharma and admired for the simplicity, symmetry and balance that mark Central Javanese work against the later East Javanese manner. Its name derives from a Javanese word for kitchen, from a root meaning dust, and it may have served as a mortuary temple for a king; bodhisattva and tara reliefs adorn its walls. Restored in 1835 under Raffles, it was inscribed with the Borobudur Temple Compounds as a World Heritage Site in 1991.

name: Candi Sukuh
deity: Shiva, represented by a lingga, with fertility and ancestor symbolism
significance: Built about 1437, a date given as a chronogram on its western gate, this temple on the slopes of Mount Lawu takes the form of a truncated stepped pyramid on three terraces, a trapezoidal plan unlike anything else among Java's classical monuments. Its carving is openly concerned with fertility, sexuality and ancestor worship, and the temple departs from the Wastu Vidya canon because it was raised as Hindu practice on Java was already weakening. It belongs to the last phase of temple building before the island's courts turned to Islam in the sixteenth century; when Raffles visited in 1815 he found the statues damaged and the great lingga broken.

name: Candi Cetho
significance: A terraced fifteenth-century Javanese-Hindu temple at 1,495 metres on the western slope of Mount Lawu, on the boundary between Central and East Java, and one of a small group built on these slopes in the same period. Like nearby Sukuh it departs sharply from the Indian-derived forms of the eighth to tenth centuries, and it belongs to the last significant phase of temple building in Java before the island's courts converted to Islam in the sixteenth century.

name: Gedong Songo
significance: Nine small Shaiva shrines arranged in five groups along 1,270 metres of hillside near Mount Ungaran, dating to the eighth or ninth century in the early Mataram period of Central Java, with scholars variously placing them around 780 to 830 or later in the ninth century. All are dedicated to Shiva and Parvati, the third group pairing a Shiva temple with Nandi and Parvati shrines, and all follow a square sanctum plan with cube-shaped cellas and multi-storeyed superstructures. Dutch archaeologists found the site badly ruined in the nineteenth century; inscriptions of 1382, 1449 and 1452 show later activity, and much restoration has been done in recent decades.

name: Candi Penataran
significance: The largest Hindu temple complex in East Java, about 12 kilometres north-east of Blitar, built up between the twelfth and fifteenth centuries with work starting in 1197 in the Kediri era and continuing through the Majapahit period. Its main temple is dedicated to Shiva, while its reliefs range widely over Vaishnava material, particularly Rama and Krishna narratives, and its three successive courtyards anticipate the arrangement of Balinese puras. It is named in the Nagarakretagama, and King Hayam Wuruk is recorded as having made it his favourite sanctuary.

name: Candi Singhasari
significance: A thirteenth-century syncretic Hindu-Buddhist temple raised as the funerary monument of Kertanagara, last king of the Singhasari dynasty, who ruled from 1268 to 1292; a large original image of Shiva as Bhatara Guru stands in the lower southern chamber and a second cella above carries the Buddhist dedication. It is named in the Nagarakretagama and in the Gajah Mada inscription of 1351, and was never finished, as the incomplete kala head over the lower entrance shows. King Chulalongkorn of Siam visited in 1896 and took away a four-armed Ganesha now in the Bangkok National Museum.

name: Candi Jago
deity: King Vishnuvardhana, deified as Shiva in the form of Avalokiteshvara
significance: A thirteenth-century Hindu-Buddhist temple of the Singhasari kingdom about 22 kilometres from Malang, commemorating King Vishnuvardhana deified as Shiva in the form of the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara; the name Adityawarman appears on a Manjushri image of 1343 found here. The Nagarakretagama of the fourteenth century calls it majestic and records a visit by King Hayam Wuruk on royal progress. Its bas-reliefs run through four narrative cycles, read anticlockwise in the prasawya manner.
story: Among the reliefs are scenes of King Angling Dharma, remembered as able to understand the speech of animals, alongside Tantri fables that teach moral lessons through animal characters.

name: Tirta Empul
significance: A Balinese Hindu water temple near Tampaksiring founded about 962 under the Warmadewa dynasty and dedicated to Vishnu, built around a sacred spring that is the source of the Pakerisan river. The precinct divides into three sections, with purification pools fed by some thirty spouts where pilgrims still perform the melukat bathing rite. A villa was built on the hill overlooking the temple for President Sukarno's visit in 1954.

name: Goa Gajah
significance: The Elephant Cave near Ubud, a rock-cut meditation sanctuary usually dated to the ninth century, though on stylistic grounds the shrine itself may belong to the eleventh-century Bali Kingdom. Lingam and yoni and an image of Ganesha stand within the cave, while stupas and chattra carved nearby show Buddhist use alongside the Shaiva. Dutch archaeologists rediscovered the site in 1923 and the bathing pool and its fountain figures were uncovered in 1954; the place is mentioned in a Javanese poem of 1365.
story: One local account holds that the cave was gouged out by the fingernail of the legendary giant Kebo Iwa.

name: Gunung Kawi
deity: Rock-cut memorial shrines to King Anak Wungsu and his queens
significance: An eleventh-century funerary complex at Tampaksiring, north-east of Ubud, where ten candi are cut in relief into seven-metre niches in the cliffs on both banks of the Pakerisan river. The shrines are understood to commemorate King Anak Wungsu of the Udayana line and his favoured queens, with the eastern group associated with King Udayana, Queen Mahendradatta and their sons. A legible inscription on the northern shrine reads Haji Lumahing Jalu, taken to mean that the king made a temple here.

name: Pura Ulun Danu Bratan
deity: Dewi Danu, goddess of lake and river; main meru to Shiva and Parvati
significance: A Shaivite water temple built in 1633 on the shore of Lake Bratan near Bedugul in central Bali, honouring Dewi Danu, goddess of the waters, with an eleven-tiered pelinggih meru dedicated to Shiva and Parvati and a Buddha image also enshrined. Laid out on a square plan with three courtyards behind decorated gates and thatched pagoda-roofed merus, it sits at the head of the irrigation system that supplies the region, linked to downstream temples belonging to each subak or irrigation society.
story: Because its shrines stand on small islets, the temple appears to float when the level of the lake rises, which is why it is popularly called the Bali temple on the lake.

name: Pura Lempuyang Luhur
significance: A hilltop sanctuary on Mount Lempuyang in eastern Bali, it is the seventh and highest of the temples in the Lempuyang complex and is counted among the island's nine holiest places of worship, revered as the guardian of the eastern direction.

name: Pura Taman Ayun
deity: Hindu gods and the ancestors of the Mengwi royal house
significance: A moated royal temple laid out in three courtyards with ranks of tiered meru towers, raised in 1634 by Gusti Agung Putu, king of Mengwi, to honour his ancestors; renovated in 1750 and again in 1937, it was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2012 as part of Bali's subak cultural landscape.

name: Pura Goa Lawah
significance: Built at the mouth of a bat-filled sea cave on the Klungkung coast and founded in the eleventh century by Mpu Kuturan, one of the priests who established Hinduism on Bali; one of its three meru towers is dedicated to Shiva, and the site became a strategic position during the 1849 War of Kusamba between the Klungkung kingdom and the Dutch colonial army.
story: The cave is held to be the domain of Naga Basuki, a primordial dragon believed to keep the balance of the cosmos.

name: Muara Takus
significance: A Mahayana Buddhist temple and stupa complex in inland Riau raised under the Srivijaya empire in the eleventh century and substantially reworked in the twelfth, serving as both a religious and a trading centre; recorded by European surveyors from 1860 and mapped by archaeologists in 1983, it is now a protected national monument.

name: Muaro Jambi Temple Compounds
significance: An extensive red-brick Buddhist temple precinct strung along the Batang Hari river, built up by the Melayu kingdom as it became Sumatra's dominant economic power in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries; the site was abandoned after a Singhasari attack in 1278 and rediscovered in 1824.

name: Arulmigu Balathandayuthapani Temple
significance: Penang's principal Murugan temple, known as the Waterfall Hilltop Temple: a shrine at the foot of the waterfall from about 1800 became the island's Thaipusam focal point, was relocated uphill after land was bought in 1914, and was rebuilt on a raised site from 2006 with a 21.6 m seven-tier gopuram, consecrated on 29 June 2012.
story: The temple's golden vel recalls the tale of the spear forged by Shiva's consort Parasakthi in eighteen forms that fused into a single indestructible weapon and was given to Murugan.

name: Nattukkottai Chettiar Temple, Penang
significance: A Murugan temple in George Town founded around 1854, after Penang's Nattukottai Chettiar community bought the land for residential quarters; its roof recesses carry hundreds of devotional paintings brought from India.

name: Sri Kandaswamy Kovil, Brickfields
significance: Founded by Kuala Lumpur's Ceylon Tamil community, which met to establish it in 1890, bought the Jalan Scott land in 1901 and held the first Maha Kumbabhishekam in February 1909; the temple maintains Saiva Siddhanta practice and was modelled on the Nallur Kandaswamy temple in Jaffna.

name: Sam Poh Tong Temple
significance: A Mahayana temple built inside a limestone cave at Ipoh, taken as a meditation hermitage in 1890 by a monk from China who lived there until his death and kept up by monks and nuns after him; the present temple buildings date from the 1950s, and the cave paintings blend Buddhist, Taoist and Hindu imagery.

name: Sri Srinivasa Perumal Temple
deity: Venkateswara (Srinivasa Perumal), a form of Vishnu
significance: One of Singapore's oldest Hindu temples, raised by early Tamil settlers on land bought in 1851 and finished in 1855; first known as Sri Narasimha Perumal Temple, it gained its five-tier gopuram in 1966 through the gift of the migrant merchant P. Govindasamy Pillai and was gazetted a national monument in 1978.

name: Sri Veeramakaliamman Temple
significance: A Little India temple to the fierce form of Kali, begun as a shrine by Bengali labourers in 1855 and built as a temple in 1881, following South Indian Tamil rather than northeastern Indian conventions; during the Japanese occupation it sheltered and fed more than twenty destitute people a night through the air raids.

name: Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Museum
deity: Buddha (sacred tooth relic); halls to Maitreya, Guanyin, Manjushri and Samantabhadra
significance: A temple and museum complex on South Bridge Road in Chinatown, completed in 2007 to enshrine a relic venerated as a tooth of the Buddha; its abbot Ven. Shi Fa Zhao rejected nine earlier proposals before settling on a northern Chinese design drawn from Tang-dynasty Buddhist architecture, with Japanese and Tibetan touches in some rooms.

name: Sri Thendayuthapani Temple
significance: Built at Tank Road in 1859 by Singapore's Chettiar community and still run by the Chettiars' Temple Society, the Murugan temple was wholly reconstructed at a cost of S$3.3 million and reconsecrated in November 1983, renovated again in 2022, and gazetted as Singapore's 67th national monument in 2014; its Thaipusam observances draw devotees carrying kavadi and milk pots.

name: Udayagiri and Khandagiri Caves
significance: Two facing sandstone ridges honeycombed with 33 part-natural, part-cut cells that housed Jain ascetics from the 2nd–1st century BCE, most of them excavated under King Kharavela. Udayagiri's Hathigumpha carries the long inscription that is the principal record of Kharavela's reign, and the Khandagiri caves were later reworked in the 11th century under the Somavamshis.

name: Kedareswar Temple
significance: One of the eight Astasambhu Shiva shrines of Bhubaneswar, standing about forty metres south of the Mukteswar temple within the Kedara-Gouri complex. Its pancharatha plan pairs a rekha vimana with a pidha jagamohana, and the sanctum floor sits below the present ground level.
story: Local telling holds that the lovers Kedar and Gouri fled their village, that Kedar was killed by a tiger and Gouri drowned herself in the pond here, and that the king raised the temple in their memory.

name: Megheswar Temple
significance: A twelfth-century Shiva shrine in the Tankapani Road quarter of Bhubaneswar, one of the many medieval deulas that survive outside the city's better-known temple cluster. Reporting in 2011 flagged the structure as threatened by waterlogging.

name: Rameshwar Deula
significance: A ninth-century Shiva shrine about two kilometres from the Lingaraj temple, known locally as the Mausi Maa or aunt's temple of Lingaraj. During the Ashokashtami festival Lingaraj is drawn here on the Rukuna Rath chariot and stays four days.
story: It is said that on returning from Lanka, Sita asked Rama to worship Shiva at this spot, and Rama set up a linga for the purpose.

name: Yameshwar Temple
significance: A sandstone Shiva temple of the Eastern Ganga period at Jameshwar Patna in Bhubaneswar, its rekha vimana paired with a pidha jagamohana and a detached mandapa inside a laterite enclosure. The sanctum holds a linga set in a circular yonipitha; parts of the fabric have weathered badly.

name: Kichakeshwari Temple
significance: Tutelary goddess of the Bhanja rulers at Khiching, their old capital, the shrine is built entirely of black chlorite and enshrines a ten-armed Chamunda-Kali. The present rekha vimana is a 1934 reconstruction by Maharaja Pratap Chandra Bhanj Deo; an attached museum founded in 1922 is the second-oldest in Odisha.

name: Varahi Deula, Chaurasi
significance: A rare sandstone khakhara-order temple of the early tenth century whose barrel-vaulted roof sets it apart from the rekha and bhadra deulas around it. Its boar-faced, pot-bellied Varahi seated in lalitasana with a fish and bowl is counted among the finest images of the goddess anywhere in India, and tantric rites including a daily fish offering continue here.

name: Simhanath Temple
significance: An early ninth-century Shiva temple at Gopinathpur in Baramba, important as an early example of the pancharatha deula with a rekha sanctuary and terraced jagamohana. Unusually it carries both Shaiva and Vaishnava sculpture and follows a panchayatana layout with subsidiary shrines to Vishnu, Ganesha, Surya and Mahishamardini.

name: Leaning Temple of Huma
significance: A Shiva temple on a rock shelf above the Mahanadi some 23 km from Sambalpur, rebuilt by the Chauhan king Baliar Singh and extended under Ajit Singh, with an earlier foundation credited to Anangabhima Deva III. It is one of very few deliberately noted leaning temples in the world, tilting about 13.8 degrees while its finial stays vertical; whether river scour or earthquake caused the tilt is unresolved.
story: A milkman is said to have crossed the river daily to pour milk on a bare rock here, which drank it each time, and the temple was raised where the miracle happened.

name: Harishankar Temple
significance: Set on the slopes of the Gandhamardan hills in Balangir, this shrine joins Vishnu and Shiva in a single dedication. The deity is said to have been found in the fourteenth century by a Chauhan king of the Patna kingdom and the temple raised at the order of queen Durlabha Devi; the plateau between it and Nrusinghanath holds Buddhist ruins associated with the ancient Parimalgiri seat of learning.

name: Akhandalamani Temple
significance: A major Shiva shrine on the bank of the Baitarani at Aradi in Bhadrak, roughly 150 feet high. An earlier wooden temple credited to Raja Niladri Samara Singha Mohapatra was replaced between 1830 and 1840 by the present masonry structure raised by Harihara Bhanja of Kanika and his chief queen Satyabhama Patadei, using stone quarried at Lalitgiri.
story: A ploughing peasant is said to have struck a black stone that bled milk and was found hooded by a cobra; the king then dreamt of Akhandalamani's arrival and built the first wooden shrine over it.

name: Panchalingeswar Temple
significance: A hilltop shrine near the Nilagiri hills named for the five Shivalingas set inside it, over which a perennial stream runs and continuously bathes them. Worshippers lie flat on the rock beside the stream to reach and touch the lingas in their natural basin.
story: One account credits Sita with installing the lingas during the exile; another says the asura king Banasura worshipped these self-manifested lingas here for the beauty of the place.

name: Maa Tarini Temple, Ghatgaon
significance: One of Odisha's most visited Shakti shrines, its establishment traced to about 1475 CE in the reign of Purushottama Deva of Kalinga and credited to his general Govinda Bhanja. The temple marks the absorption of a tribal goddess cult into mainstream Hindu worship in the Keonjhar uplands.
story: The king is said to have carried the goddess from Puri on the condition that he never look back; hearing her ornaments fall silent in the forest at Ghatgaon he turned, and she stayed there for good.

name: Biranchinarayan Temple, Buguda
significance: Known as the Wooden Konark, this Ganjam sun temple was renovated in 1790 by Srikara Bhanjadeva and counts as Odisha's second major Surya shrine after Konark. Its wooden principal image, forty-six carved pillars and chariot with seven horses driven by Aruna face west, so that the setting sun falls on the god's feet.

name: Sarala Temple
significance: The shrine of Maa Sarala at Jhankad in Jagatsinghpur district, one of the principal Shakti temples of coastal Odisha and the goddess after whom the medieval Odia poet Sarala Das is named.

name: Madan Mohan Temple
significance: Built between 1885 and 1889 by Maharaja Nripendra Narayan and opened on 21 March 1890, this is the principal temple of Cooch Behar. Madan Mohan is the kuladevata of the Koch dynasty, worshipped here in two forms, and the temple's Raas Utsav continues a fair over two centuries old.

name: Bahulara Ancient Temple
significance: A 19.2 m brick rekha deul on the Dwarakeswar river, called by Nalini Bhattasali probably the finest medieval brick deul in Bengal, with cut-brick and lime-stucco ornament. Archaeology points to an earlier Jain or Buddhist shrine on the site, later reconsecrated to Shiva; carvings of Parshvanatha and Mahishasuramardini survive on it, and it is an ASI monument of national importance.

name: Jatar Deul
significance: A near-hundred-foot brick rekha deul standing alone in the Sundarbans, found by land surveyors in the mid-nineteenth century and now an ASI monument of national importance. A lost inscription said to be dated 975 CE is attributed to Raja Jayantachandra; the sanctum held no image when recorded, and whether it began as Hindu or Buddhist is still debated.

name: Ichhai Ghosher Deul
significance: A late-medieval brick sikhara temple about 18 m high near Gourangapur, now an ASI monument of national importance. Its windowless sanctum holds no image and traces of plaster survive on the outer walls; scholars date it to the sixteenth or seventeenth century, well after the chieftain whose name it carries.
story: Tradition says the local chieftain Ichai Ghosh raised the temple in honour of the goddess Bhagabati.

name: Kanak Durga Temple
significance: A goddess shrine on the Dulung river some 14 km from Jhargram, founded roughly five centuries ago by Gopinath Singh, the feudal ruler of Chilkigarh, who is said to have made the image after a dream. The original idol was stolen twice in 2007–08 and replaced with an ashtadhatu figure; the surrounding sacred grove is now a protected herbal forest.
story: Villagers hold that human sacrifice was offered here until the goddess herself forbade it, and that on Navami she cooks the offerings with her own hands.

name: Birla Mandir, Kolkata
significance: A cream-sandstone temple on Ballygunge's Ashutosh Chowdhury Avenue built by the Birla family over twenty-six years, designed by Nomi Bose and executed under Sompura temple architects, with a silhouette echoing the Lingaraj temple of Bhubaneswar. Consecrated on 21 February 1996, it stands on 44 kathas and carries carved panels of the Bhagavad Gita, with side shrines to Durga and Shiva.

name: Calcutta Jain Temple
significance: A Shvetambara complex of four shrines at Badridas Temple Street, built in 1867 by the philanthropist Rai Badridas Bahadoor Mookim and consecrated by Acharya Kalyansuri. The main shrine to Shitalanatha is famous for mirror-inlaid pillars, stained glass, mosaic and glass chandeliers, and a ghee lamp said to have burned since 1867; the complex also holds the footprints of the monks Jinadattasuri and Jinkushalsuri.

name: Vikramashila
significance: One of the three great Pala mahaviharas alongside Nalanda and Odantapuri, founded by Dharmapala at Antichak near Kahalgaon and reputedly set up in response to a perceived decline at Nalanda. Its excavated plan is a huge square monastery of 208 cells around a cruciform stupa; it taught over a thousand students and was destroyed around 1193 by Bakhtiyar Khalji, its history preserved largely in Tibetan sources such as Taranatha.

name: Odantapuri
significance: The second-oldest of India's mahaviharas after Nalanda, founded at Bihar Sharif under Gopala I and sustained by later Pala kings and the Pithipatis of Magadha, teaching both Hinayana and Mahayana. It declined in the eleventh century and was sacked around 1193 by Bakhtiyar Khalji.
story: Tibetan tradition tells of a yogi and a Buddhist lay devotee performing a corpse rite to conjure the gold that paid for the monastery.

name: Sujata Stupa
significance: A brick stupa across the Falgu from Bodh Gaya marking the spot where the milkmaid Sujata is said to have fed the Buddha, first raised in the second century BCE and last enlarged in the ninth century under the Pala king Devapala, whose name was found inscribed here. An Ashokan pillar once stood beside it before being moved to Bodh Gaya in 1956; the ASI excavated the mound in 1973–74 and again in 2001–06.
story: Sujata of Bakraur offered milk-rice to the emaciated Gautama at this spot, ending his years of fasting and setting him on the Middle Way to enlightenment.

name: Lauria Nandangarh
significance: A Mauryan site in West Champaran with fifteen stupa mounds in three rows and a ten-metre polished sandstone Ashokan pillar crowned by a lion and carrying Brahmi edicts. Excavations by Cunningham, Bloch and Majumdar recovered figurines, pottery and, inside a miniature stupa, a birch-leaf manuscript of Buddhist text.
story: Some hold that the 26 m brick mound is the stupa in which the Buddha's ashes were enshrined.

name: Son Bhandar Caves
builtDisplay: Maurya period; dedicatory inscription 4th c. CE
significance: Two man-made Jain caves cut into the Vaibhar hill at Rajgir, the main one rectangular with a trapezoidal doorway and vaulted ceiling in the manner of the Barabar caves but less finely finished. A dedicatory inscription of about the fourth century CE credits the Jain monk Vairadeva with their excavation, while some scholars push the cutting back to the Mauryan period; a chaumukha of the seventh or eighth century shows Ajitanatha, Sambhavanatha, Shantinatha and Rishabhanatha.

name: Mangla Gauri Temple
significance: A hilltop Shakta shrine on Mangalagauri hill in Gaya, counted among the eighteen maha Shakta pithas and named in the Padma, Vayu and Agni Puranas. The present rock-cut temple dates to the fifteenth century and is credited to Maadho Giri Ji Maharaj; subsidiary shrines to Kali, Ganesha, Hanuman and Shiva stand in the complex, an unusual Shakta focus in a city dominated by Vaishnava pilgrimage.

name: Deo Sun Temple
style: Nagara with Dravida and Vesara elements
significance: Bihar's best-known sun temple and the focus of enormous Chhath gatherings each year, dated by the ASI to the fifth or sixth century, with a 1437 inscription recording a dedication by King Bhairavendra. It faces west toward the setting sun rather than east, and some scholars argue it began as a Buddhist shrine before being reconsecrated to Surya.
story: Local tradition says Vishwakarma, the divine architect, raised the whole temple in a single night.

name: Aranya Devi Temple, Arrah
deity: Aranya Devi (Aranyani, a form of Adishakti)
significance: The tutelary goddess of Arrah, whose name the town is said to carry, enshrined at Sheesh Mahal Chowk in Bhojpur district and revered as a siddha pitha alongside the 108 Shakti Pithas. The present temple was established in 2005 and a 108-foot structure was under construction as of 2022.
story: It is told that Rama and Lakshmana bathed and worshipped here with Vishvamitra on the way to Janakpur, and that Yudhishthira installed the goddess's image during the Pandavas' exile.

name: Jagannath Temple, Ranchi
significance: A smaller Kalinga-style echo of the Puri temple raised on a hillock about 10 km outside Ranchi and completed on 25 December 1691 by Ani Nath Shahdeo of Barkagarh Jagannathpur. Damaged during Aurangzeb's reign in the same year, it collapsed in August 1990 and was rebuilt by February 1992; its Rath Yatra draws large tribal and non-tribal crowds.

name: Pahari Mandir
significance: A Shiva shrine on a 2,140-foot hill in Ranchi, once called Tiriburu, whose summit the British used as a gallows for freedom fighters. K. C. Das raised the tricolour here at independence, said to be the first temple in the country to fly the national flag, and a stone on the hill records 14–15 August 1947; it fills with pilgrims at Shivaratri and through Sawan.

name: Kauleshwari Temple
significance: A tenth-century goddess shrine on the 1,575-foot Kolhua hill in Chatra district, revered as a Shakta pitha. The hill is unusual for carrying Hindu, Jain and Buddhist associations together, including a footprint attributed to the Jain tirthankara Parshvanatha and a Jain temple built in 1682, destroyed and later rebuilt.
story: Devotees hold that the womb of Sati fell on this hill, and that the Pandavas, and later Rama with Sita and Lakshmana, sheltered here during their forest exiles.

name: Bambleshwari Temple
significance: A goddess shrine on a 1,600-foot hill at Dongargarh reached by about a thousand steps or a ropeway, with a second temple, Chhotti Bambleshwari, on level ground half a kilometre away. It is one of Chhattisgarh's largest Navaratri pilgrimages, drawing hundreds of thousands of devotees.
story: Tradition tells of the childless king Veersen granted a son, Madansen, by Shiva and Parvati, after which he built the temple; another account has the goddess appearing to stop Vikramaditya from taking his own life.

name: Narayanpal Temple
significance: A Vishnu temple of about 1111 CE near the meeting of the Indravati and Narangi rivers, some four kilometres east of Chitrakote falls, built by Mumunda Devi, a queen of the Chindaka Naga line. Devanagari inscriptions at the site record a land grant to a Lokeswar by the queen-mother Gunda Mahadevi, and the Nagara superstructure shows Chalukya influence.

name: Siddheshwar Mandir, Palari
significance: A west-facing brick Shiva temple on a stellate plan at Palari, dated to about the middle of the seventh century, roughly fifty years after the Lakshmana temple at Sirpur. Its carved stone doorway carries Brahma, Vishnu, Ganga and Yamuna, and the tower is worked with gavakshas crowned by lions.

name: Mata Kaushalya Temple
significance: Described as the only temple anywhere dedicated to Kaushalya, who is shown holding the infant Rama, at Chandkhuri about 27 km from Raipur. Damaged and rebuilt repeatedly, it was renovated in 1973 and rededicated in October 2021 as the centrepiece of the Ram Van Gaman Path circuit through the old Dandakaranya country.

name: Ugratara Devalaya
significance: A Shakta shrine at Uzan Bazaar in Guwahati built in Saka 1647, or 1725 CE, by the Ahom king Siva Singha. It has no image in the sanctum: a small water-filled pit is worshipped as the goddess, who is also identified with the Buddhist Taras Tikshna-Kanta and Eka-Jata; an earlier Kamarupa Pala association has been suggested but is not supported by inscriptions.
story: The goddess is said to mark where the navel of Sati fell, and a Kamarupa legend tells of Yama complaining that no soul from the region reached hell, after which Ugra Tara was set to drive its people out until the sage Vasishtha, seized while meditating, cursed her.

name: Doul Govinda Temple
significance: A Krishna temple with an attached namghar on the north bank of the Brahmaputra at Rajaduar, established more than a century and a half ago around an image brought from Sandhyasar near Nalbari by Ganga Ram Barooah, and renovated in 1966. Its five-day Holi observance draws some five thousand pilgrims.

name: Devrani Jethani Temple Complex
significance: Two ruined sixth-century temples at Tala on the Maniyari river, among the most important surviving architecture of the Dakshina Kosala region, excavated by the ASI between 1977 and 1988. The smaller Devrani shrine carries an elaborate figured doorway and shows southern influence while the larger Jethani follows northern convention and appears to have been an experiment that collapsed; a five-tonne, 2.7 m Rudra Shiva figure covered in animal and human faces was found buried here on 17 January 1988.

name: Harihar Dham
significance: A 25-acre river-girt temple site at Bagodar in Giridih district, about a kilometre off the Grand Trunk Road, built around a 65-foot Shivalinga described as the tallest in the world and said to have taken some thirty years to complete. It fills with pilgrims at Shravan Poornima and is a favoured venue for Hindu weddings.

name: Dah Parvatiya
significance: The oldest datable temple remains in Assam, exposed at Tezpur when the 1897 earthquake destroyed a later Ahom-period brick temple built over them and excavated in 1924. The surviving carved stone door frame, with the river goddesses Ganga and Yamuna on its jambs, is regarded as the finest and earliest sculpture in the state and is protected by the ASI.

name: Negheriting Shiva Doul
significance: A hillock temple near Dergaon whose original stone shrine of the eighth or ninth century was lost to floods and shifting river courses; the linga was recovered from the shallows of the Dihing and the Ahom king Rajeswar Singha raised the present brick temple over it in 1765. It follows a panchayatana plan with corner shrines to Vishnu, Ganesha, Surya and Durga around a three-foot Banalinga, and is a nationally protected monument.
story: A sage named Urba is said to have wished to found a second Kashi here and to have gathered many Shiva lingas on the spot.

name: Hatimura Temple
significance: A Shakta shrine at Jakhalabandha in Nagaon district built in Sakabda 1667, that is 1745–46 CE, by the Ahom king Pramatta Singha, and long an important centre of goddess worship in Assam. Historical accounts record that human sacrifice was once offered at its altars.

name: Auniati Satra
significance: The first satra taken under Ahom royal patronage and one of the four raj satras, founded on Majuli about 1653 with Niranjana Deva Goswami as its first satradhikar under king Sutamla, later Jayadhwaj Singha. Belonging to the Brahma Sanghati of Ekasarana Dharma and housing celibate monks, it did much to formalise the Hinduisation of the Ahom court and holds nearly 150 historical manuscripts and royal artefacts.

name: Golden Pagoda, Namsai
significance: A Burmese-style Theravada temple on a twenty-hectare campus in Namsai district, completed in 2010 at the initiative of the local MLA Chowna Mein. The World Tripitaka Foundation is developing it as India's first international Tripitaka centre, and it hosts the Kathina Civara Dana, Sangken and Loi-Krathong observances of the Tai Khamti community.

name: Dubdi Monastery
significance: The oldest monastery in Sikkim, founded in 1701 above Yuksom, where the three lamas had crowned Phuntsog Namgyal as the first Chogyal in 1642. A two-storeyed square stone building facing south under a tapering tower, its name means the retreat; it once housed thirty monks and remains a stop on the Buddhist pilgrimage circuit.

name: Phodong Monastery
significance: One of the three principal Karma Kagyu monasteries of Sikkim founded at the instance of the ninth Karmapa, alongside Rumtek and Ralang, established in 1740 under Chogyal Gyurmed Namgyal and later rebuilt by Sidkeong Tulku Namgyal. It lies 28 km from Gangtok, houses around 260 monks and is known for its old murals.

name: Urgelling Monastery
significance: A small monastery below Tawang founded in 1489 by Urgen Sangpo, remembered above all as the birthplace of the sixth Dalai Lama, Tsangyang Gyatso, born there on 1 March 1683. An inscription at the site records the birth.

name: Ralang Monastery
significance: A Kagyu monastery six kilometres from Ravangla in South Sikkim, founded in 1768 and rebuilt between 1975 and 1981, with the new Palchen Choeling Monastic Institute completed in 1995 by the twelfth Gyaltsab Rinpoche. It holds an extensive collection of paintings and thangkas, and the older Karma Rabtenling monastery still stands nearby.

name: Sanga Choeling Monastery
significance: One of the oldest monasteries in Sikkim, founded above Pelling in 1701 by Lhatsun Namkha Jikme, its name meaning the island of the Guhyamantra, that is Vajrayana, teachings. Burnt and rebuilt several times, it still holds seventeenth-century clay images and belongs to the pilgrimage circuit that includes Pemayangtse and Tashiding; residence is restricted to male practitioners.

name: Agartala Jagannath Mandir
significance: A nineteenth-century temple in the grounds of Ujjayanta Palace at Agartala, built by Maharaja Radha Kishore Manikya on an octagonal base rising through four storeys to bright orange stepped shikharas. Its blend of Hindu, Buddhist and Islamic forms is characteristic of Tripura's court architecture, and its Ratha Yatra is now the state's principal such celebration.

name: Dashavatara Temple, Deogarh
significance: One of the earliest surviving stone temples in India, standing in the Betwa valley and carrying the ornate relief programme of the Gupta period. It is a key reference point for tracing how the north Indian temple form developed.

name: Nagvasuki Temple
significance: A riverside shrine at Daraganj on the Ganga in Prayagraj, traced to the 10th century and rebuilt in the 18th by the Maratha ruler Shridhar Bhonsle. It draws large crowds at Nag Panchami and also houses images of Shiva, Parvati and Ganesha.
story: Vasuki served as the churning rope at the Samudra Manthana and afterwards rested at the Prayag sangam, where his wounds are said to have healed.

name: Gola Gokaran Nath Temple
significance: The Shiva shrine that gives the town of Gola Gokarannath in Lakhimpur Kheri district its name. Large numbers of pilgrims gather here through the month of Sawan and at Mahashivratri.
story: Ravana is said to have pressed the linga with his thumb on his journey, leaving a mark shaped like a cow's ear, gau-karna, from which the place is named.

name: Chandrika Devi Temple, Lucknow
significance: A goddess temple on the bank of the Gomti at Bakshi Ka Talab in Lucknow district, holding nine images of Durga. It fills with pilgrims at Navratri and on new-moon nights.
story: The goddess is said to have shown herself in the hollow of an old neem tree at the site.

name: Tarkulha Devi Temple
deity: Tarkulha Devi, a form of Durga
significance: A Durga shrine in Gorakhpur district bound up with the 1857 uprising: the rebel leader Bandhu Singh took the goddess as his chosen deity and worshipped here before his raids on the British. He was hanged on 12 August 1857, and the temple keeps his memory.

name: Bijethua Mahavir
significance: A busy Hanuman temple in Sultanpur district of eastern Uttar Pradesh, noted for carrying more votive bells than any other temple in the region.
story: The Ramayana account places Hanuman's killing of the demon Kalanemi at this spot.

name: Shantinath Temple, Deogarh
significance: The principal shrine of the Deogarh Jain group, thirty-one temples holding some two thousand sculptures, the largest such assemblage anywhere. Badly damaged in earlier centuries, the site has been looked after by the Jain community since 1939.

name: Sas-Bahu Temples, Gwalior
deity: Vishnu as Aniruddha in the larger shrine; Shiva in the smaller
significance: Twin eleventh-century temples inside Gwalior Fort raised by King Mahipala, the larger for his Vaishnava queen and the smaller for her Shaiva daughter-in-law. Both were heavily damaged in later invasions, and only the larger survives with much of its elevation intact.

name: Teli ka Mandir
deity: Shiva, with Vishnu and the Matrikas
style: Nagara with a Valabhi-type barrel-vaulted roof
